column1: Already primed in memory or repeated often

column3: judging likelihood by how easily examples come to mind.
column4:
1) After viewing plane-crash news, you think flying is super risky. 
2) You overestimate shark attacks after a viral video. 
3) You think your city is “crimey” because you saw 3 crime posts.
4) You assume a test is “impossible” becauseyou remember the hardest question. 
5) You think a brand is “everywhere” because you just noticed it a lot while walking around town

A person assumes plane crashes are more common than car accidents because plane crashes get more dramatic news coverage. (Tversky & Kahneman, 1973) https://doi.org/10.1016/0010-0285(73)90033-9
A reader overestimates how common shark attacks are after watching a week of shark-themed news stories. (Tversky & Kahneman, 1973) https://doi.org/10.1016/0010-0285(73)90033-9
A person judges that more English words start with the letter K than have K as the third letter, even though the opposite is actually true, because words starting with K come to mind more easily. (Tversky & Kahneman, 1973) https://doi.org/10.1016/0010-0285(73)90033-9
A new parent overestimates the likelihood of a child being kidnapped by a stranger because of vivid news stories, even though such cases are statistically rare. (Tversky & Kahneman, 1973) https://doi.org/10.1016/0010-0285(73)90033-9
A person assumes their city has high crime rates after watching several violent local news segments in one week. (Tversky & Kahneman, 1973) https://doi.org/10.1016/0010-0285(73)90033-9
A juror judges a particular crime as more common than it really is because a similar case was recently in the headlines. (Tversky & Kahneman, 1973) https://doi.org/10.1016/0010-0285(73)90033-9
An investor overestimates the chance of a market crash right after reading a vivid news story about one, even though the underlying statistical odds haven't changed. (Tversky & Kahneman, 1973) https://doi.org/10.1016/0010-0285(73)90033-9
A student assumes essay topics about a recent historical event are likely to appear on an exam simply because that topic feels fresh and memorable. (Tversky & Kahneman, 1973) https://doi.org/10.1016/0010-0285(73)90033-9
A traveler overestimates the danger of flying after a recent plane crash dominates the news, despite flying remaining statistically very safe. (Tversky & Kahneman, 1973) https://doi.org/10.1016/0010-0285(73)90033-9
A person believes natural disasters are becoming more frequent because recent disaster coverage comes to mind quickly. (Tversky & Kahneman, 1973) https://doi.org/10.1016/0010-0285(73)90033-9
A doctor overestimates the likelihood of a rare disease in a patient because they recently treated a similar case that stands out vividly in memory. (Tversky & Kahneman, 1973) https://doi.org/10.1016/0010-0285(73)90033-9
A consumer assumes a product brand is more popular than it actually is because its commercials are especially memorable. (Tversky & Kahneman, 1973) https://doi.org/10.1016/0010-0285(73)90033-9
A voter overestimates how common a certain type of crime is in their state because a politician's ad repeatedly highlighted dramatic examples. (Tversky & Kahneman, 1973) https://doi.org/10.1016/0010-0285(73)90033-9
A person believes more deaths are caused by terrorism than by heart disease, even though heart disease kills far more people, because terrorism is more vivid and memorable. (Tversky & Kahneman, 1973) https://doi.org/10.1016/0010-0285(73)90033-9
A homeowner overestimates the chance of a house fire right after hearing about a neighbor's fire, even though their own risk factors haven't changed. (Tversky & Kahneman, 1973) https://doi.org/10.1016/0010-0285(73)90033-9
A teacher assumes cheating is rampant in their class after catching one especially memorable case, even without broader evidence. (Tversky & Kahneman, 1973) https://doi.org/10.1016/0010-0285(73)90033-9
A social media user assumes a certain political opinion is more widely held than it actually is because posts expressing it keep appearing in their feed. (Tversky & Kahneman, 1973) https://doi.org/10.1016/0010-0285(73)90033-9
A parent overestimates the danger of a particular playground toy after reading one viral injury story, even though injury rates for that toy are low. (Tversky & Kahneman, 1973) https://doi.org/10.1016/0010-0285(73)90033-9
A person assumes lottery winners are more common than they are because winning stories get widely publicized while the millions of losing tickets do not. (Tversky & Kahneman, 1973) https://doi.org/10.1016/0010-0285(73)90033-9
A manager overestimates how often a certain mistake happens on their team because one especially memorable incident sticks out vividly. (Tversky & Kahneman, 1973) https://doi.org/10.1016/0010-0285(73)90033-9
column5:
1) You check base rates (stats) before deciding. 
2) You remember the news is selective, not typical. 
3) You sample multiple sources, not just what you recall. 
4) You use actual frequencies (e.g., accident rates). 
5) You deliberately recall non-salient examples too.

A statistician calculates the actual base rates of plane crashes versus car accidents using government transportation data, correctly concluding driving is more dangerous. (Tversky & Kahneman, 1973) https://doi.org/10.1016/0010-0285(73)90033-9
A researcher counts the actual frequency of words with K in the first versus third position and accurately reports that third-position K is more common. (Tversky & Kahneman, 1973) https://doi.org/10.1016/0010-0285(73)90033-9
A city official reviews actual crime statistics over five years and accurately concludes that crime rates have been declining despite recent news coverage. (Tversky & Kahneman, 1973) https://doi.org/10.1016/0010-0285(73)90033-9
An investor reviews historical market data and accurately assesses the statistical probability of a crash, unaffected by a recent dramatic news story. (Tversky & Kahneman, 1973) https://doi.org/10.1016/0010-0285(73)90033-9
A public health official reviews actual mortality data and accurately informs the public that heart disease kills far more people than terrorism. (Tversky & Kahneman, 1973) https://doi.org/10.1016/0010-0285(73)90033-9
A doctor orders a proper diagnostic test rather than relying on memory of a recent vivid case, accurately diagnosing the patient based on actual symptoms and lab results. (Tversky & Kahneman, 1973) https://doi.org/10.1016/0010-0285(73)90033-9
A traveler checks official aviation safety statistics and accurately concludes flying remains very safe, despite a recent crash dominating headlines. (Tversky & Kahneman, 1973) https://doi.org/10.1016/0010-0285(73)90033-9
A teacher reviews grading records across the whole class and accurately concludes that cheating is rare, despite one memorable incident. (Tversky & Kahneman, 1973) https://doi.org/10.1016/0010-0285(73)90033-9
A consumer checks independent sales data and accurately concludes a heavily advertised brand is actually less popular than its quieter competitor. (Tversky & Kahneman, 1973) https://doi.org/10.1016/0010-0285(73)90033-9
A homeowner consults fire department statistics for their specific neighborhood and accurately assesses their actual fire risk, unaffected by a neighbor's recent fire. (Tversky & Kahneman, 1973) https://doi.org/10.1016/0010-0285(73)90033-9
A pollster reviews a large, representative survey and accurately reports the true distribution of political opinions, rather than relying on what shows up most in their own social feed. (Tversky & Kahneman, 1973) https://doi.org/10.1016/0010-0285(73)90033-9
A parent reviews official consumer safety data and accurately concludes a toy is statistically very safe, despite one viral injury story. (Tversky & Kahneman, 1973) https://doi.org/10.1016/0010-0285(73)90033-9
A lottery analyst calculates the true odds of winning and accurately reports them as extremely low, unaffected by widely publicized winner stories. (Tversky & Kahneman, 1973) https://doi.org/10.1016/0010-0285(73)90033-9
A manager reviews actual error logs across the whole team and accurately concludes that a certain mistake is rare, despite one especially memorable incident. (Tversky & Kahneman, 1973) https://doi.org/10.1016/0010-0285(73)90033-9
A juror weighs formal evidence and statistics presented in court, accurately avoiding being swayed by an unrelated, vivid news story about a similar crime. (Tversky & Kahneman, 1973) https://doi.org/10.1016/0010-0285(73)90033-9
A student studies the full syllabus evenly rather than over-focusing on a recently discussed topic, leading to balanced and accurate exam preparation. (Tversky & Kahneman, 1973) https://doi.org/10.1016/0010-0285(73)90033-9
A reader checks shark attack statistics from a marine research organization and accurately concludes attacks remain extremely rare despite a week of news coverage. (Tversky & Kahneman, 1973) https://doi.org/10.1016/0010-0285(73)90033-9
A voter fact-checks a political ad's crime claims against official state crime data and accurately concludes the claims were exaggerated. (Tversky & Kahneman, 1973) https://doi.org/10.1016/0010-0285(73)90033-9
A new parent consults pediatric safety statistics and accurately assesses the true, low likelihood of stranger kidnapping. (Tversky & Kahneman, 1973) https://doi.org/10.1016/0010-0285(73)90033-9
A climate scientist reviews long-term disaster frequency data and accurately distinguishes a real increasing trend from one driven merely by more media coverage. (Tversky & Kahneman, 1973) https://doi.org/10.1016/0010-0285(73)90033-9

column3: your attention is pulled toward certain cues (often threats/desires).
column4:
1) Social anxiety → you fixate on people’s frowns. 
2) Dieting → you notice every bakery. 
3) Phobia → you instantly spot spiders. 
4) Craving → you keep noticing vape shops. 
5) After a bad grade, you only see red marks.

In a study, people with anxiety disorders were slower to respond when threat-related words appeared on a screen, showing their attention was automatically drawn to those words. (MacLeod, Mathews & Tata, 1986) https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/3700842/
A person trying to quit smoking finds their eyes repeatedly drawn to cigarette packs in a store, even when trying to look elsewhere. (MacLeod, Mathews & Tata, 1986) https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/3700842/
A person on a diet finds themselves noticing every food advertisement on a billboard-lined highway, even ones they normally wouldn't register. (MacLeod, Mathews & Tata, 1986) https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/3700842/
A person with social anxiety scans a crowded room and their attention locks onto the one person who looks unfriendly, ignoring everyone smiling. (MacLeod, Mathews & Tata, 1986) https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/3700842/
A gambler trying to quit notices every casino billboard and lottery ad on their commute, even though they used to barely register them. (MacLeod, Mathews & Tata, 1986) https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/3700842/
A person with a fear of spiders spots a tiny spider in the corner of a room almost instantly, while missing other more obvious objects nearby. (MacLeod, Mathews & Tata, 1986) https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/3700842/
A worker worried about layoffs finds their attention snapping to any mention of "budget cuts" in a company-wide email, skimming past everything else. (MacLeod, Mathews & Tata, 1986) https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/3700842/
A person recovering from a breakup notices their ex's name everywhere, on playlists, in conversations, and on social media, more than they did before. (MacLeod, Mathews & Tata, 1986) https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/3700842/
A person with health anxiety reads a list of symptoms and their eyes go straight to the ones that match how they currently feel. (MacLeod, Mathews & Tata, 1986) https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/3700842/
A shopper trying to save money finds their attention repeatedly drawn to "sale" signs throughout a store, even when not looking for anything specific. (MacLeod, Mathews & Tata, 1986) https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/3700842/
A person with a fear of public speaking scans an audience and their eyes fixate on the one person checking their phone, ignoring the many engaged listeners. (MacLeod, Mathews & Tata, 1986) https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/3700842/
A person with depression reading a performance review notices and dwells on the single critical comment, while barely registering several positive ones. (MacLeod, Mathews & Tata, 1986) https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/3700842/
A new parent finds their attention snapping instantly to any unusual sound in the house, while normal background noise barely registers. (MacLeod, Mathews & Tata, 1986) https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/3700842/
A recovering alcoholic finds their attention drawn to wine displays at the grocery store, even when actively trying to focus on their shopping list. (MacLeod, Mathews & Tata, 1986) https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/3700842/
A person with test anxiety scans an exam and their eyes lock onto the hardest-looking question first, increasing their stress before reading easier ones. (MacLeod, Mathews & Tata, 1986) https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/3700842/
A person worried about their relationship notices every instance of their partner being on their phone, while overlooking the many moments of quality time together. (MacLeod, Mathews & Tata, 1986) https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/3700842/
A job seeker scrolling through listings finds their eyes drawn instantly to the word "rejected" in an email subject line before reading anything else. (MacLeod, Mathews & Tata, 1986) https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/3700842/
A person with a phobia of heights walking near a balcony finds their attention fixated on the edge, unable to focus on the view or conversation around them. (MacLeod, Mathews & Tata, 1986) https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/3700842/
In a dot-probe study, participants with anxiety reacted faster to targets that appeared where a threatening word had just been, showing their attention had shifted there automatically. (MacLeod, Mathews & Tata, 1986) https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/3700842/
A person on a strict budget finds themselves noticing prices on every single item in a store, even ones they have no intention of buying. (MacLeod, Mathews & Tata, 1986) https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/3700842/
column5:
1) Mindfully re-focus on the whole scene. 
2) You notice neutral cues equally. 
3) You use checklists to scan systematically. 
4) You practice exposure and attention training. 
5) You can describe positives and negatives evenly.

A non-anxious participant in a dot-probe study responds at roughly the same speed to threat words and neutral words, showing no automatic attentional pull toward threat. (MacLeod, Mathews & Tata, 1986) https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/3700842/
A person who has fully quit smoking walks past a cigarette display without their attention being drawn to it at all. (MacLeod, Mathews & Tata, 1986) https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/3700842/
A person without test anxiety reads through an exam in order, giving each question equal initial attention regardless of difficulty. (MacLeod, Mathews & Tata, 1986) https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/3700842/
A diner notices a food advertisement because it is unusually large and colorful, not because of any heightened personal sensitivity to food-related cues. (MacLeod, Mathews & Tata, 1986) https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/3700842/
A worker reads a company email thoroughly and notices the budget cut mention along with every other section equally, without it jumping out disproportionately. (MacLeod, Mathews & Tata, 1986) https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/3700842/
A person without arachnophobia notices a spider in the room only after specifically being told to look for it, same as any other object. (MacLeod, Mathews & Tata, 1986) https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/3700842/
A person who has fully processed a breakup can read their ex's name in a group chat without any noticeable shift in attention or mood. (MacLeod, Mathews & Tata, 1986) https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/3700842/
A reader without health anxiety scans a list of symptoms evenly, giving no particular weight to ones that vaguely match how they feel. (MacLeod, Mathews & Tata, 1986) https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/3700842/
A confident public speaker scans the audience and notices the engaged listeners and the distracted ones in roughly equal measure. (MacLeod, Mathews & Tata, 1986) https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/3700842/
An employee reads a performance review and weighs the positive and critical comments proportionally, without one critical line dominating their attention. (MacLeod, Mathews & Tata, 1986) https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/3700842/
A shopper with a clear, fixed budget notices sale signs only when relevant to their actual shopping list, not compulsively throughout the store. (MacLeod, Mathews & Tata, 1986) https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/3700842/
A recovered gambler can drive past casino billboards without any noticeable increase in attention compared to other roadside ads. (MacLeod, Mathews & Tata, 1986) https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/3700842/
A new parent who has settled into a routine sleeps through normal household sounds, only waking for genuinely unusual noises, like any well-rested adult. (MacLeod, Mathews & Tata, 1986) https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/3700842/
A secure partner notices their significant other on their phone without it triggering any disproportionate worry or attentional fixation. (MacLeod, Mathews & Tata, 1986) https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/3700842/
A person with a fear of heights who has completed exposure therapy can stand near a balcony and engage normally in conversation without fixating on the edge. (MacLeod, Mathews & Tata, 1986) https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/3700842/
A job seeker opens an email and reads the full content calmly before reacting, rather than fixating instantly on any single word. (MacLeod, Mathews & Tata, 1986) https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/3700842/
A recovering alcoholic who has built strong coping skills can walk through a grocery store's wine aisle while staying focused entirely on their shopping list. (MacLeod, Mathews & Tata, 1986) https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/3700842/
A confident professional reads a critical email and processes it calmly and proportionately, without their attention snapping to a single negative word. (MacLeod, Mathews & Tata, 1986) https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/3700842/
A driver notices a billboard simply because it is brightly lit at night, a normal visual response unrelated to any personal sensitivity. (MacLeod, Mathews & Tata, 1986) https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/3700842/
A treated patient with a former phobia of public speaking scans a room and registers it evenly, with no single audience member capturing disproportionate attention. (MacLeod, Mathews & Tata, 1986) https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/3700842/

column3: repeated statements feel more true, even if false.
column4:
1) A rumor seems believable after hearing it 10 times. 
2) Repeated ad claims feel “factual.”
 3) “Everyone says…” makes a myth stick. 
4) Reposting a misquote makes it seem real. 
5) Catchy slogans feel like evidence.

A person starts believing a piece of fake news is true simply because they have seen it shared multiple times on social media. (Hasher, Goldstein & Toppino, 1977) https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8116821/
In the original study, participants rated repeated trivia statements as more truthful than new statements, regardless of whether the statements were actually true or false. (Hasher, Goldstein & Toppino, 1977) https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8116821/
A voter starts to believe a repeated political claim simply because they have heard it stated so many times in ads. (Hasher, Goldstein & Toppino, 1977) https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8116821/
A consumer believes an advertising slogan's claim about a product simply because they have heard it dozens of times on the radio. (Hasher, Goldstein & Toppino, 1977) https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8116821/
A student begins to believe an inaccurate historical "fact" simply because a teacher repeated it multiple times throughout the semester. (Hasher, Goldstein & Toppino, 1977) https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8116821/
A reader rates a repeated health myth as more believable the second and third time they encounter it, even without any new supporting evidence. (Hasher, Goldstein & Toppino, 1977) https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8116821/
A person starts to believe a coworker's exaggerated story simply because they have heard the same version repeated at several office gatherings. (Hasher, Goldstein & Toppino, 1977) https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8116821/
A news consumer rates a repeated but unverified rumor as increasingly credible each time it resurfaces in their feed. (Hasher, Goldstein & Toppino, 1977) https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8116821/
A person who knows a piece of misinformation is false still rates it as feeling more true after seeing it repeated several times, according to research on the effect. (Hasher, Goldstein & Toppino, 1977) https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8116821/
A child starts believing an urban legend simply because they've heard the same story from multiple classmates. (Hasher, Goldstein & Toppino, 1977) https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8116821/
A jury member finds a repeated but unsubstantiated claim from a lawyer's opening statement increasingly believable by the time of closing arguments. (Hasher, Goldstein & Toppino, 1977) https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8116821/
A person becomes more confident that a wildly inaccurate weather rumor is true after hearing several different neighbors repeat it. (Hasher, Goldstein & Toppino, 1977) https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8116821/
A reader rates a conspiracy theory as more plausible the third time they encounter it online than the first, despite no new evidence being presented. (Hasher, Goldstein & Toppino, 1977) https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8116821/
A customer believes a salesperson's repeated claim about a product's durability simply because it was said multiple times during the pitch. (Hasher, Goldstein & Toppino, 1977) https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8116821/
A person begins to accept a repeated but false statistic about crime rates simply because they have heard it cited in several different conversations. (Hasher, Goldstein & Toppino, 1977) https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8116821/
A reader rates a repeated celebrity rumor as more credible after the third or fourth time it appears in different gossip articles. (Hasher, Goldstein & Toppino, 1977) https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8116821/
A social media user starts to question their own correct knowledge after seeing an inaccurate claim repeated by several different accounts. (Hasher, Goldstein & Toppino, 1977) https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8116821/
A study participant rated a false trivia statement as true after hearing it three times across separate sessions, even though it contradicted things they already knew. (Hasher, Goldstein & Toppino, 1977) https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8116821/
A person becomes more convinced that a debunked health remedy works simply because they keep seeing it repeated across different wellness blogs. (Hasher, Goldstein & Toppino, 1977) https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8116821/
A listener starts believing an inaccurate sports statistic simply because a commentator has repeated it across several broadcasts. (Hasher, Goldstein & Toppino, 1977) https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8116821/
column5:
1) You verify with reliable sources. 
2) you base your claims off given data. 
3) You check original data. 
4) You label claims as “unverified.” 
5) You change your belief when evidence contradicts it.

A fact-checker rates a claim's truthfulness based on verified evidence, giving the same accurate assessment whether they have seen the claim once or many times. (Hasher, Goldstein & Toppino, 1977) https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8116821/
A scientist evaluates a repeated but unverified hypothesis using controlled experiments rather than how many times they have heard it stated. (Hasher, Goldstein & Toppino, 1977) https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8116821/
A voter checks an independent fact-checking site and correctly rejects a political claim as false despite hearing it repeated in many ads. (Hasher, Goldstein & Toppino, 1977) https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8116821/
A consumer remains skeptical of an advertising slogan and looks up independent product reviews before forming a belief, regardless of how often the slogan is repeated. (Hasher, Goldstein & Toppino, 1977) https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8116821/
A student double checks an inaccurate "fact" from a teacher against a primary historical source and correctly identifies the error. (Hasher, Goldstein & Toppino, 1977) https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8116821/
A reader consults a medical journal to verify a health claim, correctly identifying it as false regardless of how many times they have seen it shared. (Hasher, Goldstein & Toppino, 1977) https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8116821/
A person hears a coworker's exaggerated story repeated several times but recognizes inconsistencies in the details and correctly doubts its accuracy. (Hasher, Goldstein & Toppino, 1977) https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8116821/
A news consumer traces a repeated rumor back to its unreliable original source and correctly concludes it is unsubstantiated. (Hasher, Goldstein & Toppino, 1977) https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8116821/
A jury member bases their verdict strictly on admitted evidence, correctly disregarding a repeated but unsupported claim from an attorney's opening statement. (Hasher, Goldstein & Toppino, 1977) https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8116821/
A child checks an urban legend against a trusted adult's explanation and correctly concludes it is not true, despite hearing it from several classmates. (Hasher, Goldstein & Toppino, 1977) https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8116821/
A researcher rates statements based on logical consistency and evidence rather than how many times they have encountered them. (Hasher, Goldstein & Toppino, 1977) https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8116821/
A customer asks for independent third-party reviews and correctly identifies a salesperson's repeated durability claim as exaggerated. (Hasher, Goldstein & Toppino, 1977) https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8116821/
A statistician checks a repeated crime statistic against official government data and correctly identifies it as inaccurate. (Hasher, Goldstein & Toppino, 1977) https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8116821/
A reader cross-references a celebrity rumor with reputable entertainment journalism and correctly dismisses it despite seeing it repeated. (Hasher, Goldstein & Toppino, 1977) https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8116821/
A social media user fact-checks an inaccurate claim before accepting or rejecting it, regardless of how many accounts have repeated it. (Hasher, Goldstein & Toppino, 1977) https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8116821/
A study participant correctly rates a repeated false statement as false because it directly contradicts verified personal expertise in that subject area. (Hasher, Goldstein & Toppino, 1977) https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8116821/
A person consults a licensed doctor and correctly rejects a debunked health remedy, despite seeing it repeated across many wellness blogs. (Hasher, Goldstein & Toppino, 1977) https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8116821/
A listener checks an official sports statistics database and correctly identifies a commentator's repeated claim as inaccurate. (Hasher, Goldstein & Toppino, 1977) https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8116821/
A teacher explicitly warns students that a commonly repeated myth is false, and students correctly retain the accurate information instead. (Hasher, Goldstein & Toppino, 1977) https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8116821/
A reader who is a subject matter expert immediately recognizes a repeated claim as false the very first time they encounter it, based on their own expertise. (Hasher, Goldstein & Toppino, 1977) https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8116821/

column3: familiarity increases liking.
column4:
You like a song more after more listens.
A classmate seems nicer after seeing them often.
A logo feels more trustworthy because it’s familiar.
You start preferring a style you see repeatedly.
A catchphrase becomes appealing over time.

A person develops a liking for a song they initially found annoying simply after hearing it played repeatedly on the radio. (Zajonc, 1968) https://cdn.isr.umich.edu/pubFiles/historicPublications/Theattitudinaleffects_2360_.PDF
In Zajonc's classic study, participants rated nonsense words and Chinese characters more favorably the more times they had been shown them, even with no understanding of their meaning. (Zajonc, 1968) https://cdn.isr.umich.edu/pubFiles/historicPublications/Theattitudinaleffects_2360_.PDF
A voter develops a more favorable impression of a candidate simply from seeing their campaign signs repeatedly around town. (Zajonc, 1968) https://cdn.isr.umich.edu/pubFiles/historicPublications/Theattitudinaleffects_2360_.PDF
A coworker who initially seemed unremarkable becomes someone a person grows fond of after months of regularly passing them in the hallway. (Zajonc, 1968) https://cdn.isr.umich.edu/pubFiles/historicPublications/Theattitudinaleffects_2360_.PDF

column3: A general tendency to perceive meaningful connections or patterns where none objectively exist.
column4:
Reading a sign into a coincidence with nothing behind it.
Treating unrelated events as parts of one hidden pattern.
Finding meaning in what chance alone produced.
Deciding a run of coincidences cannot be coincidence.
Connecting unrelated details into a single deliberate design.

After three unrelated acquaintances died in the same month, a man decided deaths genuinely arrive in threes, treating a coincidence as a pattern with meaning behind it.
A conspiracy theorist connects unrelated dates, initials and coincidences into one deliberate plot, and treats the absence of any link between them as proof the connection was concealed.
A driver sees the same three digits on a licence plate, a receipt and a door number, and reads the coincidence as a sign not to travel that day.
A gambler decides the casino runs a hidden schedule because two of his three wins fell on a Tuesday, finding a pattern in a coincidence far too small to mean anything.
Someone who wakes at 3:33 three nights running searches for the meaning in it, treating a chance repetition as a message meant for them.
A believer in numerology adds the digits of an ordinary date until they reach a number they consider fateful, reading significance into an arithmetic coincidence.
A researcher scanning hundreds of variables reports a striking correlation between cheese consumption and engineering doctorates, mistaking a chance pattern for a real connection.
Investors seized on the 'Super Bowl indicator', a coincidence between which conference wins and how the market moves, with no mechanism connecting the two.
A sports fan concludes his team only wins when he wears a particular shirt, treating four coincidental results as a pattern with a cause behind it.
A patient becomes convinced two unrelated symptoms must share one hidden cause because they happened to appear in the same week.
A trader draws trendlines across what is a random walk of prices and becomes certain a deliberate pattern is forming in the noise.
A reader notices two novels published decades apart share a minor detail and concludes one must be a coded reference to the other.
A villager treats an unusually cold spring following a comet as evidence the comet caused it, connecting two unrelated events into one story.
Someone who dreamt of an accident the night before one happened treats the coincidence as foreknowledge, forgetting every dream that matched nothing.
A fan decodes a band's album art into a message about a member's death, reading a deliberate pattern into unrelated design choices.
A gardener credits a good harvest to the phase of the moon he planted under, connecting two events that share only their timing.
An analyst finds a recurring shape in quarterly figures and forecasts from it, though that shape is what chance variation of that length produces.
A reader of a vague horoscope finds in it an exact account of an argument from the day before, taking wording that fits anyone as meant for them.
An investigator links a suspect to a crime through a chain of coincidences, each unremarkable alone, and treats the chain itself as proof.
A manager reads a deliberate rebuke into an ambiguous one-line email, finding an intended meaning in wording that carried none.
column5:
Recognising a coincidence as a coincidence.
Asking what could actually connect two unrelated events.
Accepting that chance alone produces patterns.
Checking whether a pattern survives on new data.
Treating wording that fits anyone as fitting anyone.

A statistician points out that a coincidence of that kind is exactly what chance produces in a sample that size, and that no pattern needs explaining.
A researcher who finds a striking correlation across hundreds of scanned variables treats it as a chance pattern until it survives a test on fresh data.
An analyst refuses to trade on a shape in the figures until it holds up against series known to contain nothing but random variation.
A juror asks what mechanism could connect two coincidental dates before treating the coincidence as evidence of a deliberate plot.
A reader notices their horoscope would fit almost anyone's week and stops treating its wording as meant for them.
A doctor investigates whether two symptoms appearing the same week actually share a cause rather than assuming the coincidence must mean one.
A gardener tests the harvest against plantings made at other phases of the moon, and finds the connection was only in the timing.
A gambler accepts that two of three wins falling on the same weekday is unremarkable and reads no pattern into it.
A fan concludes the album art carries no hidden message once the designer explains the unrelated choices behind it.
A manager asks the sender what an ambiguous email meant rather than reading an intended meaning into it.
An investigator notes that a chain of individually unremarkable coincidences is still a coincidence without evidence connecting them.
Someone who dreamt of an accident counts the dreams that matched nothing before treating the one that matched as meaningful.
