A voter judges a politician who fails to prevent a disaster less harshly than one who actively causes a smaller disaster of the same size. (Ritov & Baron, 1990) https://www.sas.upenn.edu/~baron/papers.htm/vac.html
An investor feels less guilty about losing money by leaving it in a failing stock than by actively moving it into a new investment that also loses money. (Ritov & Baron, 1990) https://www.sas.upenn.edu/~baron/papers.htm/vac.html
A manager avoids firing an underperforming employee because letting the problem continue feels less blameworthy than actively making the difficult call. (Ritov & Baron, 1990) https://www.sas.upenn.edu/~baron/papers.htm/vac.html
A juror rates a defendant who let someone drown as less guilty than one who actively pushed the person into the water, even though the outcome was identical. (Ritov & Baron, 1990) https://www.sas.upenn.edu/~baron/papers.htm/vac.html
A person feels less responsible for not donating to charity than for actively taking money away from a charity, even though both leave the charity with the same shortfall. (Ritov & Baron, 1990) https://www.sas.upenn.edu/~baron/papers.htm/vac.html
A company avoids proactively recalling a product with a minor known defect because taking action feels riskier than simply doing nothing and hoping for the best. (Ritov & Baron, 1990) https://www.sas.upenn.edu/~baron/papers.htm/vac.html
A student refuses to point out a classmate's cheating but feels no guilt, even though actively cheating themselves would feel far worse. (Ritov & Baron, 1990) https://www.sas.upenn.edu/~baron/papers.htm/vac.html
A patient chooses to skip a screening test rather than risk a false positive result, even though skipping the test raises the overall chance of missing a serious illness. (Ritov & Baron, 1990) https://www.sas.upenn.edu/~baron/papers.htm/vac.html
A city council delays fixing a known pothole because leaving it alone feels less risky to their reputation than approving a repair that could go wrong. (Ritov & Baron, 1990) https://www.sas.upenn.edu/~baron/papers.htm/vac.html
A person feels more comfortable ignoring a struggling friend's calls than saying something hurtful, even though both choices leave the friend feeling abandoned. (Ritov & Baron, 1990) https://www.sas.upenn.edu/~baron/papers.htm/vac.html
An engineer avoids recommending a new safety upgrade because if it fails the blame will feel worse than if the old, riskier system simply keeps running as is. (Ritov & Baron, 1990) https://www.sas.upenn.edu/~baron/papers.htm/vac.html
A pharmacist hesitates to proactively flag a borderline prescription because not acting feels less risky than actively questioning a doctor's judgment. (Ritov & Baron, 1990) https://www.sas.upenn.edu/~baron/papers.htm/vac.html
A person avoids reporting a minor safety violation at work because staying silent feels less consequential than actively speaking up and being wrong. (Ritov & Baron, 1990) https://www.sas.upenn.edu/~baron/papers.htm/vac.html
A parent lets a child skip a seasonal flu shot, reasoning that whatever illness follows will feel less like their fault than any side effect from the shot itself. (Ritov & Baron, 1990) https://www.sas.upenn.edu/~baron/papers.htm/vac.html
A hiring manager avoids promoting a qualified but unconventional candidate, since a bad outcome from inaction feels less risky than one from an active decision. (Ritov & Baron, 1990) https://www.sas.upenn.edu/~baron/papers.htm/vac.html
A person chooses not to intervene when they see a stranger being scammed, feeling less responsible than if they had actively pointed the stranger toward the scam. (Ritov & Baron, 1990) https://www.sas.upenn.edu/~baron/papers.htm/vac.html
A teacher avoids updating an outdated lesson plan because sticking with the old one feels safer than risking a new approach that could fail. (Ritov & Baron, 1990) https://www.sas.upenn.edu/~baron/papers.htm/vac.html
A driver avoids honking to warn another car of danger, feeling less at fault for staying quiet than for honking and being wrong. (Ritov & Baron, 1990) https://www.sas.upenn.edu/~baron/papers.htm/vac.html
column5:
You judge by outcome and responsibility, not action/inaction.
You treat omissions as choices with consequences.
You choose the least-harm option even if it’s active.
You use expected-value thinking.
You act when inaction predictably harms.

A parent vaccinates their child right away after weighing the numbers, showing no reluctance at all once the risk of the disease is clearly explained as far higher than the risk of the vaccine. (Ritov & Baron, 1990) https://www.sas.upenn.edu/~baron/papers.htm/vac.html
A doctor recommends the statistically safer treatment regardless of whether it requires action or inaction, judging purely by the numbers. (Ritov & Baron, 1990) https://www.sas.upenn.edu/~baron/papers.htm/vac.html
A juror rates a person who let a friend drown just as guilty as one who pushed them in, focusing only on the outcome rather than whether the harm came from action or inaction. (Ritov & Baron, 1990) https://www.sas.upenn.edu/~baron/papers.htm/vac.html
An investor moves their money out of a failing stock the moment new data shows a better option, without hesitating over whether the loss came from action or inaction. (Ritov & Baron, 1990) https://www.sas.upenn.edu/~baron/papers.htm/vac.html
A manager fires an underperforming employee quickly because company policy weighs outcomes rather than whether the harm came from acting or not acting. (Ritov & Baron, 1990) https://www.sas.upenn.edu/~baron/papers.htm/vac.html
A city council approves a pothole repair immediately once the numbers show the cost of an accident outweighs the cost of the fix. (Ritov & Baron, 1990) https://www.sas.upenn.edu/~baron/papers.htm/vac.html
A person avoids donating to a certain charity simply because they distrust its finances, which is a judgment about the charity rather than a preference for inaction. (Ritov & Baron, 1990) https://www.sas.upenn.edu/~baron/papers.htm/vac.html
A patient skips a screening test because their doctor genuinely advised against it due to a low personal risk profile, not because of any reluctance to act. (Ritov & Baron, 1990) https://www.sas.upenn.edu/~baron/papers.htm/vac.html
An engineer recommends the safety upgrade without hesitation once the data clearly shows it reduces the accident rate. (Ritov & Baron, 1990) https://www.sas.upenn.edu/~baron/papers.htm/vac.html
A company recalls a defective product immediately, treating a failure to act as just as serious as a mistake made by acting. (Ritov & Baron, 1990) https://www.sas.upenn.edu/~baron/papers.htm/vac.html
A student reports a classmate's cheating right away because they believe staying silent is just as wrong as cheating themselves. (Ritov & Baron, 1990) https://www.sas.upenn.edu/~baron/papers.htm/vac.html
A driver honks immediately to warn another car of danger without weighing whether staying silent would feel safer for their own reputation. (Ritov & Baron, 1990) https://www.sas.upenn.edu/~baron/papers.htm/vac.html
A pharmacist questions a borderline prescription right away, treating silence as equally risky as speaking up. (Ritov & Baron, 1990) https://www.sas.upenn.edu/~baron/papers.htm/vac.html
A hiring manager promotes the most qualified candidate without hesitation, applying the same standard regardless of whether the decision involves action or inaction. (Ritov & Baron, 1990) https://www.sas.upenn.edu/~baron/papers.htm/vac.html
A person intervenes immediately when they see a stranger being scammed, treating staying silent as just as bad as helping the scam along. (Ritov & Baron, 1990) https://www.sas.upenn.edu/~baron/papers.htm/vac.html
A teacher updates an outdated lesson plan right away once research shows the new approach genuinely helps students learn better. (Ritov & Baron, 1990) https://www.sas.upenn.edu/~baron/papers.htm/vac.html
A parent skips a seasonal flu shot for their child purely because a doctor found a genuine allergy risk, not out of any general reluctance to act. (Ritov & Baron, 1990) https://www.sas.upenn.edu/~baron/papers.htm/vac.html
A voter judges a politician who failed to prevent a disaster just as harshly as one who actively caused a disaster of the same size. (Ritov & Baron, 1990) https://www.sas.upenn.edu/~baron/papers.htm/vac.html
A person speaks up right away about a safety violation at work, seeing silence as just as risky as being wrong. (Ritov & Baron, 1990) https://www.sas.upenn.edu/~baron/papers.htm/vac.html
Most participants in a classic study showed no preference at all between harmful action and harmful inaction once the response scale was designed to remove any built in bias. (Ritov & Baron, 1990) https://www.sas.upenn.edu/~baron/papers.htm/vac.html

column3: ignoring overall odds (base rates) when judging probability.
column4:
“Shy person” → assume librarian, ignoring job proportions.
Think a rare disease is likely after one symptom.
Overtrust a “positive” test without considering rarity.
One scammy text → assume all texts are scams.
Vivid story → you overestimate a rare event.

A person hears that a witness correctly identifies a cab's color eighty percent of the time and assumes there is an eighty percent chance the cab really was that color, ignoring that most cabs in the city are a different color entirely. (Bar-Hillel, 1980) http://bear.warrington.ufl.edu/brenner/mar7588/Papers/barhillel-acta1980.pdf
A hiring manager reads a personality description that sounds like an engineer and assumes the candidate is probably an engineer, ignoring that the applicant pool is mostly lawyers. (Bar-Hillel, 1980) http://bear.warrington.ufl.edu/brenner/mar7588/Papers/barhillel-acta1980.pdf
A patient who tests positive on a rare disease screening assumes they definitely have the disease, ignoring how rare the disease actually is in the general population. (Bar-Hillel, 1980) http://bear.warrington.ufl.edu/brenner/mar7588/Papers/barhillel-acta1980.pdf
A juror hears that a fingerprint matches with ninety nine percent accuracy and assumes the suspect is almost certainly guilty, ignoring how many innocent people could also share a similar partial match in a large city. (Bar-Hillel, 1980) http://bear.warrington.ufl.edu/brenner/mar7588/Papers/barhillel-acta1980.pdf
A teacher assumes a shy new student is probably struggling academically because shy students seem to fit that stereotype, ignoring how few shy students in the school actually struggle. (Bar-Hillel, 1980) http://bear.warrington.ufl.edu/brenner/mar7588/Papers/barhillel-acta1980.pdf
An airport security officer flags a nervous looking traveler as a likely threat, ignoring how overwhelmingly rare actual threats are compared to ordinary nervous travelers. (Bar-Hillel, 1980) http://bear.warrington.ufl.edu/brenner/mar7588/Papers/barhillel-acta1980.pdf
A recruiter assumes a candidate with a confident interview style is more likely to succeed in the role, ignoring that only a small fraction of confident interviewees actually perform well on the job. (Bar-Hillel, 1980) http://bear.warrington.ufl.edu/brenner/mar7588/Papers/barhillel-acta1980.pdf
A doctor tells a patient that a positive cancer screening test means they probably have cancer, without factoring in how rare that cancer is among people the patient's age. (Bar-Hillel, 1980) http://bear.warrington.ufl.edu/brenner/mar7588/Papers/barhillel-acta1980.pdf
A news reader assumes plane crashes are common after seeing a dramatic headline, ignoring the extremely low base rate of crashes compared to the number of flights each day. (Bar-Hillel, 1980) http://bear.warrington.ufl.edu/brenner/mar7588/Papers/barhillel-acta1980.pdf
A loan officer assumes an applicant with tattoos is a higher credit risk based on a personality impression, ignoring the actual default rate data for that group. (Bar-Hillel, 1980) http://bear.warrington.ufl.edu/brenner/mar7588/Papers/barhillel-acta1980.pdf
A social media user assumes a scary sounding side effect is common after reading one viral post, ignoring how rare that side effect actually is according to clinical data. (Bar-Hillel, 1980) http://bear.warrington.ufl.edu/brenner/mar7588/Papers/barhillel-acta1980.pdf
A detective focuses on a suspect whose behavior matches a criminal stereotype, ignoring how many innocent people also share that same behavior. (Bar-Hillel, 1980) http://bear.warrington.ufl.edu/brenner/mar7588/Papers/barhillel-acta1980.pdf
A parent assumes a video game must be dangerous because it resembles a game linked to one rare tragic story, ignoring how many millions of people play it safely. (Bar-Hillel, 1980) http://bear.warrington.ufl.edu/brenner/mar7588/Papers/barhillel-acta1980.pdf
A student assumes a described stranger is more likely to be an artist than an accountant because the description sounds creative, without considering that far more accountants exist in the population being sampled. (Bar-Hillel, 1980) http://bear.warrington.ufl.edu/brenner/mar7588/Papers/barhillel-acta1980.pdf
An HR analyst assumes an employee who fits a "quiet high performer" description is likely one of the company's top earners, without checking how rare that title actually is among all quiet employees. (Bar-Hillel, 1980) http://bear.warrington.ufl.edu/brenner/mar7588/Papers/barhillel-acta1980.pdf
A shopper assumes a product with one dramatic bad review is generally unsafe, ignoring how few complaints exist relative to total units sold. (Bar-Hillel, 1980) http://bear.warrington.ufl.edu/brenner/mar7588/Papers/barhillel-acta1980.pdf
A voter assumes voter fraud is widespread after hearing about one local case, ignoring the extremely small number of confirmed cases compared to millions of votes cast. (Bar-Hillel, 1980) http://bear.warrington.ufl.edu/brenner/mar7588/Papers/barhillel-acta1980.pdf
A manager assumes an applicant who studied a certain major will definitely be a good fit, ignoring how few graduates of that major actually succeed in similar past roles at the company. (Bar-Hillel, 1980) http://bear.warrington.ufl.edu/brenner/mar7588/Papers/barhillel-acta1980.pdf
A therapist client assumes their unusual symptom must indicate a rare disorder just because it fits the description, ignoring that a far more common condition explains the same symptom for most people. (Bar-Hillel, 1980) http://bear.warrington.ufl.edu/brenner/mar7588/Papers/barhillel-acta1980.pdf
A researcher reading a lab report jumps to conclude a new drug works because ninety percent of responders improved, without checking how many people would have improved anyway without any treatment at all. (Bar-Hillel, 1980) http://bear.warrington.ufl.edu/brenner/mar7588/Papers/barhillel-acta1980.pdf
column5:
You start with base rates, then update with evidence.
You ask “How common is this overall?”
You use Bayesian updating.
You compute rough real-world probabilities.
You compare to population statistics.

A doctor correctly tells a patient that even a positive test for a rare disease still leaves a low overall chance of actually having it, once the rarity of the disease is factored in using natural frequencies. (Weber, Binder, & Krauss, 2018) https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC6194348/
A juror weighs a witness's identification against the actual ratio of blue to green cabs in the city and correctly estimates a lower probability than the witness's confidence alone would suggest. (Weber, Binder, & Krauss, 2018) https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC6194348/
A hiring manager correctly adjusts a confident interview impression by also checking objective performance data across many past hires. (Weber, Binder, & Krauss, 2018) https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC6194348/
A statistics student solves a screening test problem correctly by converting the percentages into natural frequencies, arriving at the accurate low probability. (Weber, Binder, & Krauss, 2018) https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC6194348/
A financial analyst correctly discounts one company's dramatic earnings report by comparing it against the average performance of similar companies in the same industry. (Weber, Binder, & Krauss, 2018) https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC6194348/
A pilot ignores a single false alarm and trusts the plane's overall safety record because they have been trained to weigh long term maintenance data over a single reading. (Weber, Binder, & Krauss, 2018) https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC6194348/
A public health official correctly explains that most positive results in a mass screening for a rare illness will actually be false alarms, based on the illness's low prevalence. (Weber, Binder, & Krauss, 2018) https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC6194348/
An engineer distrusts a single failed test result and instead relies on the long term failure rate data collected across thousands of units. (Weber, Binder, & Krauss, 2018) https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC6194348/
A teacher predicts that a shy new student will likely do fine academically, since the school's own data shows shyness has little relationship to grades. (Weber, Binder, & Krauss, 2018) https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC6194348/
A loan officer denies a loan because an applicant's actual credit history shows repeated missed payments, which is a valid use of individual evidence rather than any base rate error. (Weber, Binder, & Krauss, 2018) https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC6194348/
A detective clears a suspect who matched a stereotype after confirming an alibi with hard evidence, correctly overriding first impressions with facts. (Weber, Binder, & Krauss, 2018) https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC6194348/
A researcher correctly concludes a new drug is effective only after comparing improvement rates to a control group that received no treatment at all. (Weber, Binder, & Krauss, 2018) https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC6194348/
A shopper ignores one dramatic bad review and instead checks the product's overall average rating across thousands of buyers before deciding. (Weber, Binder, & Krauss, 2018) https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC6194348/
A voter checks official state audit reports before concluding that fraud allegations from a single anecdote are not representative of the whole election. (Weber, Binder, & Krauss, 2018) https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC6194348/
A nervous traveler is correctly cleared by airport security after additional screening shows no actual threat, following procedures designed around the true rarity of threats. (Weber, Binder, & Krauss, 2018) https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC6194348/
A therapist correctly diagnoses a common condition instead of a rare one after ruling out the more common explanation first, following standard diagnostic practice. (Weber, Binder, & Krauss, 2018) https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC6194348/
A news reader checks aviation safety statistics and correctly concludes that flying remains far safer than driving despite one dramatic headline. (Weber, Binder, & Krauss, 2018) https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC6194348/
An HR analyst confirms an employee's high performance using measurable sales numbers rather than relying on a vague personality impression. (Weber, Binder, & Krauss, 2018) https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC6194348/
A recruiter tracks long term data showing which majors actually succeed in a role and hires based on that evidence instead of assumptions. (Weber, Binder, & Krauss, 2018) https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC6194348/
A parent researches actual injury statistics before deciding a video game is safe, rather than judging it by one rare viral story. (Weber, Binder, & Krauss, 2018) https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC6194348/

column1: Strange, funny, visually striking, or anthropomorphic

column3: unusual/weird info is remembered better than ordinary info.
column4:
A weird sentence sticks where a plain one does not.
The odd detail is the part that is remembered.
Strange images outlast ordinary ones in memory.
The surreal advert is recalled; the sensible one is not.
Unusual material beats ordinary material for recall.
A student remembers the sentence "the elephant rode the bicycle down the hallway" far better than the plain sentence "the elephant walked down the hallway." (McDaniel & Einstein, 1986) https://www.researchgate.net/publication/232488701_Bizarre_Imagery_as_an_Effective_Memory_Aid_The_Importance_of_Distinctiveness
A person memorizing a grocery list recalls "the toothpaste wearing a top hat" far more easily than a plain item like "toothpaste." (McDaniel & Einstein, 1986) https://www.researchgate.net/publication/232488701_Bizarre_Imagery_as_an_Effective_Memory_Aid_The_Importance_of_Distinctiveness
In a memory experiment, volunteers who studied a mixed list of ordinary and strange sentences remembered the strange ones better at recall time. (Kroneisen, 2013) https://www.researchgate.net/publication/237057357_The_bizarreness_effect_Evidence_for_the_critical_influence_of_retrieval_processes
A marketing team finds that a weird, surreal commercial about a talking refrigerator is remembered by more viewers than a plain, ordinary ad for the same product. (McDaniel & Einstein, 1986) https://www.researchgate.net/publication/232488701_Bizarre_Imagery_as_an_Effective_Memory_Aid_The_Importance_of_Distinctiveness
A student studying for an anatomy exam remembers a bizarre mnemonic image of "a heart wearing sneakers" better than the plain term "cardiac muscle." (McDaniel & Einstein, 1986) https://www.researchgate.net/publication/232488701_Bizarre_Imagery_as_an_Effective_Memory_Aid_The_Importance_of_Distinctiveness
A jury remembers an unusual, oddly specific detail from a witness's testimony far longer than the plain, expected details. (Kroneisen, 2013) https://www.researchgate.net/publication/237057357_The_bizarreness_effect_Evidence_for_the_critical_influence_of_retrieval_processes
A language learner remembers the word for "cloud" more easily after picturing it as a "cloud eating a sandwich" instead of just repeating the word plainly. (McDaniel & Einstein, 1986) https://www.researchgate.net/publication/232488701_Bizarre_Imagery_as_an_Effective_Memory_Aid_The_Importance_of_Distinctiveness
A person remembers a coworker's odd habit of alphabetizing their snacks far longer than they remember an ordinary coworker's ordinary habits. (Kroneisen, 2013) https://www.researchgate.net/publication/237057357_The_bizarreness_effect_Evidence_for_the_critical_influence_of_retrieval_processes
A comedian's bizarre, surreal joke about a dog running for mayor sticks in the audience's memory far longer than a plain observational joke told the same night. (Kroneisen, 2013) https://www.researchgate.net/publication/237057357_The_bizarreness_effect_Evidence_for_the_critical_influence_of_retrieval_processes
A trainee remembers a strange step in a safety procedure, like "hug the fire extinguisher before use," far better than a plain instructional step. (McDaniel & Einstein, 1986) https://www.researchgate.net/publication/232488701_Bizarre_Imagery_as_an_Effective_Memory_Aid_The_Importance_of_Distinctiveness
A reader remembers an unusual plot twist in a mixed collection of short stories far better than the more predictable stories in the same book. (Kroneisen, 2013) https://www.researchgate.net/publication/237057357_The_bizarreness_effect_Evidence_for_the_critical_influence_of_retrieval_processes
A history student remembers an odd, quirky fact about a king's pet lion much better than the plain dates of his reign. (McDaniel & Einstein, 1986) https://www.researchgate.net/publication/232488701_Bizarre_Imagery_as_an_Effective_Memory_Aid_The_Importance_of_Distinctiveness
A shopper remembers an oddly shaped, unusual product packaging design far longer than an ordinary box on the same shelf. (Kroneisen, 2013) https://www.researchgate.net/publication/237057357_The_bizarreness_effect_Evidence_for_the_critical_influence_of_retrieval_processes
A memory competitor links each playing card to a bizarre image, like a whale riding a skateboard, and recalls the deck's order far better than by memorizing the cards plainly. (McDaniel & Einstein, 1986) https://www.researchgate.net/publication/232488701_Bizarre_Imagery_as_an_Effective_Memory_Aid_The_Importance_of_Distinctiveness
A patient remembers an unusual, oddly specific instruction from a doctor, like "take this pill standing on one foot," far better than a plain instruction. (McDaniel & Einstein, 1986) https://www.researchgate.net/publication/232488701_Bizarre_Imagery_as_an_Effective_Memory_Aid_The_Importance_of_Distinctiveness
A teacher notices students remember a strange, memorable example about a talking calculator far better than a standard textbook example on the same lesson. (Kroneisen, 2013) https://www.researchgate.net/publication/237057357_The_bizarreness_effect_Evidence_for_the_critical_influence_of_retrieval_processes
A traveler remembers an unusual street performer they saw once far longer than the many ordinary shops on the same street. (Kroneisen, 2013) https://www.researchgate.net/publication/237057357_The_bizarreness_effect_Evidence_for_the_critical_influence_of_retrieval_processes
A person remembers a strange dream involving a flying staircase far more vividly than an ordinary dream about walking to work. (McDaniel & Einstein, 1986) https://www.researchgate.net/publication/232488701_Bizarre_Imagery_as_an_Effective_Memory_Aid_The_Importance_of_Distinctiveness
An app designer finds that users remember an unusual, whimsical loading animation far better than a plain spinning circle. (Kroneisen, 2013) https://www.researchgate.net/publication/237057357_The_bizarreness_effect_Evidence_for_the_critical_influence_of_retrieval_processes
A student memorizing chemistry terms recalls "a nitrogen atom wearing roller skates" more easily than the plain term "nitrogen atom." (McDaniel & Einstein, 1986) https://www.researchgate.net/publication/232488701_Bizarre_Imagery_as_an_Effective_Memory_Aid_The_Importance_of_Distinctiveness
column5:
1. The weird part distracts you from the real lesson. 
2. You forget the concept but remember the silly detail. 
3. Meaningful (not weird) info is remembered better.
 4. You remember less when the weirdness is confusing. 
5. Practice/retrieval beats weirdness.

A student who studies only a list of strange, bizarre sentences with no ordinary sentences mixed in shows no memory advantage at all, since the bizarreness effect requires a mixed list to work. (Kroneisen, 2013) https://www.researchgate.net/publication/237057357_The_bizarreness_effect_Evidence_for_the_critical_influence_of_retrieval_processes
A person remembers a plain, ordinary sentence better than a bizarre one because the bizarre sentence was also more grammatically complex and harder to picture. (McDaniel & Einstein, 1986) https://www.researchgate.net/publication/232488701_Bizarre_Imagery_as_an_Effective_Memory_Aid_The_Importance_of_Distinctiveness
A worker remembers every step of a safety checklist equally well because the training used repetition and practice rather than any strange or unusual imagery. (McDaniel & Einstein, 1986) https://www.researchgate.net/publication/232488701_Bizarre_Imagery_as_an_Effective_Memory_Aid_The_Importance_of_Distinctiveness
A viewer remembers a plain, ordinary commercial jingle just as well as a strange one because the jingle was repeated so many times that repetition, not oddness, drove the memory. (Kroneisen, 2013) https://www.researchgate.net/publication/237057357_The_bizarreness_effect_Evidence_for_the_critical_influence_of_retrieval_processes
A student given semantic elaboration instructions, like judging how unusual a sentence sounds instead of picturing it, shows no memory boost from bizarre sentences at all. (McDaniel & Einstein, 1986) https://www.researchgate.net/publication/232488701_Bizarre_Imagery_as_an_Effective_Memory_Aid_The_Importance_of_Distinctiveness
A reader remembers a plot twist not because it was strange but because it was emotionally moving, which reflects an emotional memory advantage rather than bizarreness. (Kroneisen, 2013) https://www.researchgate.net/publication/237057357_The_bizarreness_effect_Evidence_for_the_critical_influence_of_retrieval_processes
A patient remembers a plain medication instruction just as well as a strange one because the pharmacist wrote both down clearly on a printed label. (McDaniel & Einstein, 1986) https://www.researchgate.net/publication/232488701_Bizarre_Imagery_as_an_Effective_Memory_Aid_The_Importance_of_Distinctiveness
A memory athlete recalls an ordinary list of numbers just as accurately as a list paired with strange images, because extensive practice with the plain method closed the gap. (Kroneisen, 2013) https://www.researchgate.net/publication/237057357_The_bizarreness_effect_Evidence_for_the_critical_influence_of_retrieval_processes
A shopper remembers an ordinary product's packaging just as well as an unusual one because the ordinary product was simply placed at eye level on the shelf. (Kroneisen, 2013) https://www.researchgate.net/publication/237057357_The_bizarreness_effect_Evidence_for_the_critical_influence_of_retrieval_processes
A teacher's strange, memorable classroom example is forgotten just as quickly as an ordinary one once tested a month later, since long delays weaken the bizarreness advantage. (Kroneisen, 2013) https://www.researchgate.net/publication/237057357_The_bizarreness_effect_Evidence_for_the_critical_influence_of_retrieval_processes
A person recalls both the strange and plain items on a list equally well when they are tested separately from each other rather than together. (Kroneisen, 2013) https://www.researchgate.net/publication/237057357_The_bizarreness_effect_Evidence_for_the_critical_influence_of_retrieval_processes
A student remembers a plain historical date better than a bizarre mnemonic because the bizarre image was too complicated to picture clearly. (McDaniel & Einstein, 1986) https://www.researchgate.net/publication/232488701_Bizarre_Imagery_as_an_Effective_Memory_Aid_The_Importance_of_Distinctiveness
A language learner recalls an ordinary vocabulary flashcard just as well as a strange mnemonic one because the ordinary card included a clear picture of the real object. (McDaniel & Einstein, 1986) https://www.researchgate.net/publication/232488701_Bizarre_Imagery_as_an_Effective_Memory_Aid_The_Importance_of_Distinctiveness
A comedian's plain observational joke gets remembered just as well as a surreal one because the plain joke was delivered with especially sharp timing. (Kroneisen, 2013) https://www.researchgate.net/publication/237057357_The_bizarreness_effect_Evidence_for_the_critical_influence_of_retrieval_processes
A person listening to an audio only version of a strange sentence shows no memory boost, since the bizarreness effect relies heavily on generating a visual image. (McDaniel & Einstein, 1986) https://www.researchgate.net/publication/232488701_Bizarre_Imagery_as_an_Effective_Memory_Aid_The_Importance_of_Distinctiveness
A jury remembers a plain, ordinary piece of testimony better than an odd detail because the plain testimony was directly tied to establishing the timeline of the crime. (Kroneisen, 2013) https://www.researchgate.net/publication/237057357_The_bizarreness_effect_Evidence_for_the_critical_influence_of_retrieval_processes
A trainee forgets a strange safety instruction just as often as a plain one when the whole training session is made entirely of unusual examples with nothing ordinary to contrast them against. (Kroneisen, 2013) https://www.researchgate.net/publication/237057357_The_bizarreness_effect_Evidence_for_the_critical_influence_of_retrieval_processes
A history student remembers a plain date better than a quirky fact because the date was tied to a personally meaningful event, like their own birthday. (McDaniel & Einstein, 1986) https://www.researchgate.net/publication/232488701_Bizarre_Imagery_as_an_Effective_Memory_Aid_The_Importance_of_Distinctiveness
An app designer's plain loading animation is remembered just as well as a whimsical one once both are shown to users hundreds of times, since repeated exposure evens out the advantage. (Kroneisen, 2013) https://www.researchgate.net/publication/237057357_The_bizarreness_effect_Evidence_for_the_critical_influence_of_retrieval_processes
A reader forgets a bizarre plot twist quickly because it did not connect logically to the rest of the story, showing that bizarreness alone does not guarantee lasting memory. (Kroneisen, 2013) https://www.researchgate.net/publication/237057357_The_bizarreness_effect_Evidence_for_the_critical_influence_of_retrieval_processes

column3: humorous material is remembered better than non-humorous material.
column4:
1. A pun helps you remember a term. 
2. A meme makes a rule stick. 
3. A funny analogy helps recall a science concept. 
4. A joke example anchors a history event.
 5. You remember a teacher’s funny line on a test.

A comedian's joke about airline food sticks in the audience's memory far longer than the plain safety announcement that came right before it. (Schmidt, 1994) https://www.researchgate.net/publication/15135502_Effects_of_Humor_on_Sentence_Memory
A student remembers a funny mnemonic rhyme about the water cycle far better than the plain textbook definition. (Schmidt, 1994) https://www.researchgate.net/publication/15135502_Effects_of_Humor_on_Sentence_Memory
A viewer remembers a witty, humorous commercial for a cleaning product far longer than a plain, straightforward ad for the same product. (Stavatir, 2010) https://psychology.yale.edu/sites/default/files/stavatir_spring2010_seniorthesis.pdf
A trainee recalls a manager's funny analogy about "herding cats" during a chaotic project far better than the plain project timeline. (Schmidt, 1994) https://www.researchgate.net/publication/15135502_Effects_of_Humor_on_Sentence_Memory
Volunteers in a memory study recalled sentences written as jokes better than the same information written in a plain, serious tone. (Schmidt, 1994) https://www.researchgate.net/publication/15135502_Effects_of_Humor_on_Sentence_Memory
A patient remembers a doctor's lighthearted joke about "eating vegetables so grandma stops worrying" far longer than the plain nutrition advice given the same visit. (Schmidt, 1994) https://www.researchgate.net/publication/15135502_Effects_of_Humor_on_Sentence_Memory
A social media user remembers a funny meme about tax season far longer than a plain reminder post about the filing deadline. (Stavatir, 2010) https://psychology.yale.edu/sites/default/files/stavatir_spring2010_seniorthesis.pdf
A jury member remembers a lawyer's one funny aside during closing arguments far longer than the plain factual summary that followed. (Schmidt, 1994) https://www.researchgate.net/publication/15135502_Effects_of_Humor_on_Sentence_Memory
A child remembers a silly, funny song about brushing teeth far better than a plain spoken instruction to brush twice a day. (Stavatir, 2010) https://psychology.yale.edu/sites/default/files/stavatir_spring2010_seniorthesis.pdf
An employee recalls a coworker's funny nickname for a broken printer far longer than the plain repair ticket number. (Schmidt, 1994) https://www.researchgate.net/publication/15135502_Effects_of_Humor_on_Sentence_Memory
A researcher finds that participants recall humorous cartoons better than literal, non-funny versions of the same cartoons. (Schmidt, 1994) https://www.researchgate.net/publication/15135502_Effects_of_Humor_on_Sentence_Memory
A voter remembers a candidate's funny one-liner from a debate far longer than the plain policy statement given right after it. (Stavatir, 2010) https://psychology.yale.edu/sites/default/files/stavatir_spring2010_seniorthesis.pdf
A student in a lecture remembers the one funny example a professor used far better than the plain, technical definition given beforehand. (Schmidt, 1994) https://www.researchgate.net/publication/15135502_Effects_of_Humor_on_Sentence_Memory
A shopper remembers a funny slogan on a cereal box far longer than the plain nutrition facts printed next to it. (Stavatir, 2010) https://psychology.yale.edu/sites/default/files/stavatir_spring2010_seniorthesis.pdf
A reader of a technology newsletter remembers the one funny pun in the headline far longer than the plain headlines around it. (Schmidt, 1994) https://www.researchgate.net/publication/15135502_Effects_of_Humor_on_Sentence_Memory
A patient remembers a nurse's funny joke about "brave face" stickers far longer than the plain post-visit instructions. (Schmidt, 1994) https://www.researchgate.net/publication/15135502_Effects_of_Humor_on_Sentence_Memory
An intern remembers a manager's funny comparison of quarterly reports to "herding cats through a hurricane" far longer than the plain spreadsheet numbers. (Schmidt, 1994) https://www.researchgate.net/publication/15135502_Effects_of_Humor_on_Sentence_Memory
A first grader recalls a funny rhyme taught during a lesson far more easily than the plain sentence taught right after it. (Stavatir, 2010) https://psychology.yale.edu/sites/default/files/stavatir_spring2010_seniorthesis.pdf
A courtroom observer remembers a witness's unintentionally funny remark far longer than the plain testimony that came before and after it. (Schmidt, 1994) https://www.researchgate.net/publication/15135502_Effects_of_Humor_on_Sentence_Memory
A reader of a science article remembers the one funny analogy about black holes "eating spaghetti" far longer than the plain technical explanation. (Schmidt, 1994) https://www.researchgate.net/publication/15135502_Effects_of_Humor_on_Sentence_Memory
column5:
1. You remember the joke but not the content. 
2. Humor derails attention and lowers learning. 
3. The joke offends → you disengage.
 4. Serious relevance beats humor for recall. 
5. You learn equally well with deliberate practice alone.

A student who studies a list made up entirely of funny sentences with nothing plain to compare them to shows no memory boost at all, since the humor effect requires a mixed list of funny and plain material. (Schmidt, 1994) https://www.researchgate.net/publication/15135502_Effects_of_Humor_on_Sentence_Memory
A reader remembers a plain, serious news headline better than a funny one because the serious headline was about a topic personally relevant to them. (Schmidt, 1994) https://www.researchgate.net/publication/15135502_Effects_of_Humor_on_Sentence_Memory
A patient remembers a doctor's plain, serious warning about medication far better than an unrelated joke told earlier in the same visit, since the warning was repeated and written down. (Schmidt, 1994) https://www.researchgate.net/publication/15135502_Effects_of_Humor_on_Sentence_Memory
A student remembers a plain definition just as well as a funny mnemonic because the plain definition was tested repeatedly through practice quizzes. (Schmidt, 1994) https://www.researchgate.net/publication/15135502_Effects_of_Humor_on_Sentence_Memory
A viewer forgets a funny commercial just as quickly as a plain one because the funny commercial's joke had nothing to do with the product itself. (Stavatir, 2010) https://psychology.yale.edu/sites/default/files/stavatir_spring2010_seniorthesis.pdf
An employee remembers a plain, direct instruction from a manager better than a joke because the plain instruction affected the employee's paycheck directly. (Schmidt, 1994) https://www.researchgate.net/publication/15135502_Effects_of_Humor_on_Sentence_Memory
A jury remembers the plain factual summary in a closing argument better than a joke because the plain summary directly matched the evidence they were asked to weigh. (Schmidt, 1994) https://www.researchgate.net/publication/15135502_Effects_of_Humor_on_Sentence_Memory
An older participant in a memory study shows little to no advantage for humorous sentences compared to plain ones, unlike younger participants in the same study. (Schmidt, 1994) https://www.researchgate.net/publication/15135502_Effects_of_Humor_on_Sentence_Memory
A child forgets a funny classroom rhyme just as quickly as a plain sentence when both are only presented once with no repetition. (Stavatir, 2010) https://psychology.yale.edu/sites/default/files/stavatir_spring2010_seniorthesis.pdf
A reader remembers a plain scientific explanation better than a funny analogy because the plain version was accompanied by a clear diagram. (Schmidt, 1994) https://www.researchgate.net/publication/15135502_Effects_of_Humor_on_Sentence_Memory
A voter forgets a candidate's joke from a debate but remembers the plain policy statement because it directly affected their own taxes. (Stavatir, 2010) https://psychology.yale.edu/sites/default/files/stavatir_spring2010_seniorthesis.pdf
A shopper remembers the plain nutrition facts on a cereal box better than the funny slogan because they were actively looking for sugar content. (Stavatir, 2010) https://psychology.yale.edu/sites/default/files/stavatir_spring2010_seniorthesis.pdf
A student under a strict warning to focus and take the material seriously shows a reduced memory boost from humorous material compared to students given no such warning. (Schmidt, 1994) https://www.researchgate.net/publication/15135502_Effects_of_Humor_on_Sentence_Memory
A patient recalls the plain post-visit instructions accurately because a nurse also handed them a printed checklist, regardless of the joke told earlier. (Schmidt, 1994) https://www.researchgate.net/publication/15135502_Effects_of_Humor_on_Sentence_Memory
A courtroom observer remembers the plain testimony details better than a witness's joke because the plain testimony was central to the verdict. (Schmidt, 1994) https://www.researchgate.net/publication/15135502_Effects_of_Humor_on_Sentence_Memory
An intern forgets a manager's funny analogy quickly because it was never repeated or written down anywhere. (Schmidt, 1994) https://www.researchgate.net/publication/15135502_Effects_of_Humor_on_Sentence_Memory
A reader remembers a plain headline better than a punny one because the plain headline appeared in bold at the very top of the page. (Schmidt, 1994) https://www.researchgate.net/publication/15135502_Effects_of_Humor_on_Sentence_Memory
A student remembers a professor's plain, technical definition better than a joke because the definition appeared on the final exam word for word. (Schmidt, 1994) https://www.researchgate.net/publication/15135502_Effects_of_Humor_on_Sentence_Memory
A first grader remembers a plain instruction to wash hands better than a funny song because a poster with the plain instruction hung right above the sink. (Stavatir, 2010) https://psychology.yale.edu/sites/default/files/stavatir_spring2010_seniorthesis.pdf
A social media user forgets a funny meme within a day because it was never shared or engaged with again after the first viewing. (Stavatir, 2010) https://psychology.yale.edu/sites/default/files/stavatir_spring2010_seniorthesis.pdf

column3: the item that stands out in a group is remembered best.
column4:
1. One red word in a black list is recalled. 
2. One odd shape among circles is noticed. 
3. One loud sound in silence is remembered. 
4. One bolded stat on a slide sticks.
 5. One unique name in a class is remembered.

A shopper remembers the one item highlighted in bright green on an otherwise plain black and white shopping list far better than any other item. (Kelley & Nairne, 2001) https://www.researchgate.net/publication/12127312_Von_Restorff_Revisited_Isolation_Generation_and_Memory_for_Order
A student studying a list of fruit names remembers "airplane" far better than any of the fruits because it stands out from the category. (Kelley & Nairne, 2001) https://www.researchgate.net/publication/12127312_Von_Restorff_Revisited_Isolation_Generation_and_Memory_for_Order
A juror remembers the one witness who wore a bright red jacket far better than any of the other witnesses dressed in plain suits. (MacLeod, 2020) https://www.researchgate.net/publication/340626696_Zeigarnik_and_von_Restorff_The_memory_effects_and_the_stories_behind_them
A reader of a dense report remembers the one sentence printed in bold and underlined far better than the surrounding plain text. (Kelley & Nairne, 2001) https://www.researchgate.net/publication/12127312_Von_Restorff_Revisited_Isolation_Generation_and_Memory_for_Order
A shopper remembers the one oddly shaped bottle on a shelf full of identical rectangular boxes far better than any of the boxes. (MacLeod, 2020) https://www.researchgate.net/publication/340626696_Zeigarnik_and_von_Restorff_The_memory_effects_and_the_stories_behind_them
A student memorizing a list of history dates remembers the one date written in a different font far better than the rest. (Kelley & Nairne, 2001) https://www.researchgate.net/publication/12127312_Von_Restorff_Revisited_Isolation_Generation_and_Memory_for_Order
An employee remembers the one slide in a presentation that used a bright red background while every other slide was plain white. (Kelley & Nairne, 2001) https://www.researchgate.net/publication/12127312_Von_Restorff_Revisited_Isolation_Generation_and_Memory_for_Order
A patient remembers the one unusually named medication on their prescription list far better than the other, more ordinary sounding drug names. (MacLeod, 2020) https://www.researchgate.net/publication/340626696_Zeigarnik_and_von_Restorff_The_memory_effects_and_the_stories_behind_them
A voter remembers the one candidate who wore a bright yellow tie in a debate lineup of otherwise dark suits far better than any other candidate. (Kelley & Nairne, 2001) https://www.researchgate.net/publication/12127312_Von_Restorff_Revisited_Isolation_Generation_and_Memory_for_Order
A driver remembers the one oddly shaped road sign among a row of standard rectangular signs far more easily than the others. (Kelley & Nairne, 2001) https://www.researchgate.net/publication/12127312_Von_Restorff_Revisited_Isolation_Generation_and_Memory_for_Order
An app designer notices users remember the one brightly colored button on an otherwise gray screen far better than any other element. (MacLeod, 2020) https://www.researchgate.net/publication/340626696_Zeigarnik_and_von_Restorff_The_memory_effects_and_the_stories_behind_them
A student memorizing vocabulary words remembers the one word written in all capital letters far better than the surrounding lowercase words. (Kelley & Nairne, 2001) https://www.researchgate.net/publication/12127312_Von_Restorff_Revisited_Isolation_Generation_and_Memory_for_Order
A reader of a legal contract remembers the one clause printed in bold and boxed off far better than the surrounding paragraphs. (Kelley & Nairne, 2001) https://www.researchgate.net/publication/12127312_Von_Restorff_Revisited_Isolation_Generation_and_Memory_for_Order
A person browsing a music playlist remembers the one instrumental track in a list of songs with lyrics far better than any of the other tracks. (MacLeod, 2020) https://www.researchgate.net/publication/340626696_Zeigarnik_and_von_Restorff_The_memory_effects_and_the_stories_behind_them
A shopper remembers the one product with a bright orange label on a shelf full of white labeled competitors. (MacLeod, 2020) https://www.researchgate.net/publication/340626696_Zeigarnik_and_von_Restorff_The_memory_effects_and_the_stories_behind_them
A student remembers the one number written in a math problem set that was printed upside down far better than any of the other numbers. (Kelley & Nairne, 2001) https://www.researchgate.net/publication/12127312_Von_Restorff_Revisited_Isolation_Generation_and_Memory_for_Order
A juror remembers the single piece of evidence presented in a strange plastic case far better than the folders full of paper evidence. (MacLeod, 2020) https://www.researchgate.net/publication/340626696_Zeigarnik_and_von_Restorff_The_memory_effects_and_the_stories_behind_them
An employee remembers the one email marked "urgent" in red font far better than the dozens of plain subject lines in their inbox that week. (Kelley & Nairne, 2001) https://www.researchgate.net/publication/12127312_Von_Restorff_Revisited_Isolation_Generation_and_Memory_for_Order
A traveler remembers the one unusually tall building on an otherwise uniform city skyline far better than the surrounding buildings. (MacLeod, 2020) https://www.researchgate.net/publication/340626696_Zeigarnik_and_von_Restorff_The_memory_effects_and_the_stories_behind_them
A teacher notices students remember the one test question printed in a different color far more often than the surrounding black and white questions. (Kelley & Nairne, 2001) https://www.researchgate.net/publication/12127312_Von_Restorff_Revisited_Isolation_Generation_and_Memory_for_Order
column5:
1. Everything is highlighted → nothing stands out. 
2. You miss it because you’re distracted. 
3. You remember first/last instead (not the standout). 
4. The standout is irrelevant so you ignore it. 
5. Understanding (not distinctness) drives recall.

A student remembers a plain, unhighlighted item on a study list just as well as a bright green one because they reviewed the plain item ten separate times before the test. (Kelley & Nairne, 2001) https://www.researchgate.net/publication/12127312_Von_Restorff_Revisited_Isolation_Generation_and_Memory_for_Order
A shopper remembers an oddly shaped bottle no better than the surrounding boxes because they were already very familiar with that unusual shape from years of buying it. (MacLeod, 2020) https://www.researchgate.net/publication/340626696_Zeigarnik_and_von_Restorff_The_memory_effects_and_the_stories_behind_them
An employee forgets the one red highlighted slide just as quickly as the plain white ones because the presentation was over an hour long and attention had already faded. (Kelley & Nairne, 2001) https://www.researchgate.net/publication/12127312_Von_Restorff_Revisited_Isolation_Generation_and_Memory_for_Order
A participant with a strong personal memory strategy shows little to no advantage in recalling an isolated item, unlike other participants without such a strategy. (Kelley & Nairne, 2001) https://www.researchgate.net/publication/12127312_Von_Restorff_Revisited_Isolation_Generation_and_Memory_for_Order
A juror remembers a plain looking witness's testimony better than a flashy dressed witness because the plain witness's account matched the physical evidence exactly. (MacLeod, 2020) https://www.researchgate.net/publication/340626696_Zeigarnik_and_von_Restorff_The_memory_effects_and_the_stories_behind_them
A reader remembers a plain sentence in a report better than the one bolded sentence because the plain sentence contained the actual dollar figures they needed for a decision. (Kelley & Nairne, 2001) https://www.researchgate.net/publication/12127312_Von_Restorff_Revisited_Isolation_Generation_and_Memory_for_Order
A driver remembers all the standard road signs equally well on a familiar daily commute regardless of any one sign's unusual shape. (Kelley & Nairne, 2001) https://www.researchgate.net/publication/12127312_Von_Restorff_Revisited_Isolation_Generation_and_Memory_for_Order
A student forgets the one capitalized vocabulary word just as quickly as the lowercase ones because none of the words were ever tested or reviewed again. (Kelley & Nairne, 2001) https://www.researchgate.net/publication/12127312_Von_Restorff_Revisited_Isolation_Generation_and_Memory_for_Order
A voter remembers a plainly dressed candidate's policy position better than a flashy dressed candidate's because the plain candidate's position directly affected the voter's own job. (Kelley & Nairne, 2001) https://www.researchgate.net/publication/12127312_Von_Restorff_Revisited_Isolation_Generation_and_Memory_for_Order
An app designer finds that a brightly colored button gets ignored by users because it was placed in a spot users never scroll to. (MacLeod, 2020) https://www.researchgate.net/publication/340626696_Zeigarnik_and_von_Restorff_The_memory_effects_and_the_stories_behind_them
A patient forgets the one unusually named medication just as easily as the ordinary ones because none of the names were explained or repeated by the pharmacist. (MacLeod, 2020) https://www.researchgate.net/publication/340626696_Zeigarnik_and_von_Restorff_The_memory_effects_and_the_stories_behind_them
A teacher's students remember a plain test question just as well as the colorful one because the plain question was explicitly flagged as likely to appear on the final exam. (Kelley & Nairne, 2001) https://www.researchgate.net/publication/12127312_Von_Restorff_Revisited_Isolation_Generation_and_Memory_for_Order
A traveler remembers all the buildings on a skyline about equally well because they were sightseeing with a guidebook that described each one in similar detail. (MacLeod, 2020) https://www.researchgate.net/publication/340626696_Zeigarnik_and_von_Restorff_The_memory_effects_and_the_stories_behind_them
An employee deletes an urgent red flagged email without reading it and later forgets it entirely, showing visual distinctiveness alone does not guarantee memory without engagement. (Kelley & Nairne, 2001) https://www.researchgate.net/publication/12127312_Von_Restorff_Revisited_Isolation_Generation_and_Memory_for_Order
A person browsing a playlist remembers a song with lyrics just as well as the one instrumental track because they replayed the lyrical song many times that week. (MacLeod, 2020) https://www.researchgate.net/publication/340626696_Zeigarnik_and_von_Restorff_The_memory_effects_and_the_stories_behind_them
A reader of a legal contract remembers an ordinary clause better than the boxed off one because a lawyer specifically explained the ordinary clause's real world consequences. (Kelley & Nairne, 2001) https://www.researchgate.net/publication/12127312_Von_Restorff_Revisited_Isolation_Generation_and_Memory_for_Order
A shopper forgets the one orange labeled product on the shelf because they were shopping quickly on autopilot and not paying close attention to any packaging. (MacLeod, 2020) https://www.researchgate.net/publication/340626696_Zeigarnik_and_von_Restorff_The_memory_effects_and_the_stories_behind_them
A student remembers an upside down number no better than the rest of the math problems because the whole worksheet was formatted in a similarly unusual style throughout. (Kelley & Nairne, 2001) https://www.researchgate.net/publication/12127312_Von_Restorff_Revisited_Isolation_Generation_and_Memory_for_Order
A juror remembers a piece of evidence in a plain folder just as well as the one in a strange plastic case because both were referenced repeatedly by the prosecutor. (MacLeod, 2020) https://www.researchgate.net/publication/340626696_Zeigarnik_and_von_Restorff_The_memory_effects_and_the_stories_behind_them
A driver forgets the one oddly shaped sign because it was positioned behind a tree and never actually seen clearly while driving past. (Kelley & Nairne, 2001) https://www.researchgate.net/publication/12127312_Von_Restorff_Revisited_Isolation_Generation_and_Memory_for_Order

column3: pictures/images are remembered better than words alone.
column4:
1. You recall a diagram better than a paragraph.
 2. Image flashcards stick more than text-only. 
3. You remember a map better than directions. 
4. A chart makes data easier to recall.
 5. You recognize faces better than names.

A student remembers a diagram of the heart far better than a paragraph of text describing the same parts of the heart. (CMU Memory Lab) https://www.cmu.edu/dietrich/psychology/memorylab/publications/10.1.1.646.3474.pdf
A shopper remembers a company's logo far longer than they remember the company's written slogan. (CMU Memory Lab) https://www.cmu.edu/dietrich/psychology/memorylab/publications/10.1.1.646.3474.pdf
A traveler remembers a photo of a landmark from a brochure far better than the written paragraph describing it. (CMU Memory Lab) https://www.cmu.edu/dietrich/psychology/memorylab/publications/10.1.1.646.3474.pdf
A patient remembers a picture of the correct pill shape and color far better than the written name of the medication. (Paivio, Rogers, & Smythe, 1968, as cited in Paivio & Csapo, 1973) https://www.researchgate.net/publication/258349100_Memory_for_pictures_and_words_as_a_function_of_level_of_processing_Depth_or_dual_coding
A jury remembers a photograph shown as evidence far longer than the written police report describing the same scene. (CMU Memory Lab) https://www.cmu.edu/dietrich/psychology/memorylab/publications/10.1.1.646.3474.pdf
A student studying for a biology exam remembers a labeled picture of a cell far better than the plain written list of its parts. (CMU Memory Lab) https://www.cmu.edu/dietrich/psychology/memorylab/publications/10.1.1.646.3474.pdf
A viewer of a safety training video remembers the picture of the correct fire extinguisher grip far better than the written instructions read aloud. (CMU Memory Lab) https://www.cmu.edu/dietrich/psychology/memorylab/publications/10.1.1.646.3474.pdf
A voter remembers a candidate's campaign photo far longer than they remember the candidate's written policy statement. (CMU Memory Lab) https://www.cmu.edu/dietrich/psychology/memorylab/publications/10.1.1.646.3474.pdf
A social media user remembers a meme's image far longer than they remember a plain text post with the same joke. (CMU Memory Lab) https://www.cmu.edu/dietrich/psychology/memorylab/publications/10.1.1.646.3474.pdf
A student learning a new language remembers a vocabulary word paired with a picture far better than the same word paired with only a written translation. (CMU Memory Lab) https://www.cmu.edu/dietrich/psychology/memorylab/publications/10.1.1.646.3474.pdf
A shopper remembers the picture on a product's packaging far longer than the written ingredient list on the same package. (CMU Memory Lab) https://www.cmu.edu/dietrich/psychology/memorylab/publications/10.1.1.646.3474.pdf
A reader of an instruction manual remembers the diagram showing how to assemble a shelf far better than the written steps next to it. (CMU Memory Lab) https://www.cmu.edu/dietrich/psychology/memorylab/publications/10.1.1.646.3474.pdf
A researcher finds that participants recall a list of pictures better than the same list presented as written words. (CMU Memory Lab) https://www.cmu.edu/dietrich/psychology/memorylab/publications/10.1.1.646.3474.pdf
A student remembers a chart showing population growth far better than the written paragraph describing the same statistics. (CMU Memory Lab) https://www.cmu.edu/dietrich/psychology/memorylab/publications/10.1.1.646.3474.pdf
A tourist remembers a picture postcard of a city far longer than they remember the written description on the back of it. (CMU Memory Lab) https://www.cmu.edu/dietrich/psychology/memorylab/publications/10.1.1.646.3474.pdf
An employee remembers an organizational chart with photos of coworkers far better than a plain written list of names and titles. (CMU Memory Lab) https://www.cmu.edu/dietrich/psychology/memorylab/publications/10.1.1.646.3474.pdf
A child remembers a picture book's illustrations far longer than they remember the plain text on the same page. (CMU Memory Lab) https://www.cmu.edu/dietrich/psychology/memorylab/publications/10.1.1.646.3474.pdf
A driver remembers a picture based road sign, like a curve symbol, far better than a written sign that says "curve ahead." (CMU Memory Lab) https://www.cmu.edu/dietrich/psychology/memorylab/publications/10.1.1.646.3474.pdf
A student remembers an infographic about climate change far better than the written article covering the same facts. (CMU Memory Lab) https://www.cmu.edu/dietrich/psychology/memorylab/publications/10.1.1.646.3474.pdf
