column5:
1. A cluttered image harms memory. 
2. Clear text beats a vague picture. 
3. Abstract ideas need language more than images.
 4. Retrieval practice makes words as memorable. 
5. Images don’t help if you don’t understand them.

A group of participants in a recognition memory study actually remembered written words better than photographs of unfamiliar faces, reversing the usual picture advantage. (CMU Memory Lab) https://www.cmu.edu/dietrich/psychology/memorylab/publications/10.1.1.646.3474.pdf
A student remembers a written definition better than a picture because the picture was unclear and did not obviously represent the concept being taught. (CMU Memory Lab) https://www.cmu.edu/dietrich/psychology/memorylab/publications/10.1.1.646.3474.pdf
A jury remembers a written witness statement better than a blurry photograph because the photograph was too low quality to make out any details. (CMU Memory Lab) https://www.cmu.edu/dietrich/psychology/memorylab/publications/10.1.1.646.3474.pdf
A reader remembers a written safety warning better than an accompanying picture because the picture used an unfamiliar symbol that was hard to interpret. (CMU Memory Lab) https://www.cmu.edu/dietrich/psychology/memorylab/publications/10.1.1.646.3474.pdf
A shopper remembers a product's written ingredient list better than its picture because they were specifically checking for an allergen by name. (CMU Memory Lab) https://www.cmu.edu/dietrich/psychology/memorylab/publications/10.1.1.646.3474.pdf
A student learning an abstract concept, like justice, remembers the written definition better than any picture, since abstract ideas are harder to represent visually. (CMU Memory Lab) https://www.cmu.edu/dietrich/psychology/memorylab/publications/10.1.1.646.3474.pdf
A voter remembers a candidate's written policy statement better than a campaign photo because the statement was repeated in multiple news articles that week. (CMU Memory Lab) https://www.cmu.edu/dietrich/psychology/memorylab/publications/10.1.1.646.3474.pdf
An employee remembers a written meeting agenda better than an accompanying stock photo because the photo had nothing to do with the meeting's content. (CMU Memory Lab) https://www.cmu.edu/dietrich/psychology/memorylab/publications/10.1.1.646.3474.pdf
A traveler remembers a written itinerary better than a generic stock photo in a brochure because the itinerary contained specific times and addresses they needed. (CMU Memory Lab) https://www.cmu.edu/dietrich/psychology/memorylab/publications/10.1.1.646.3474.pdf
A patient remembers a written medication name better than a picture of the pill because two different medications happened to look nearly identical in the picture. (CMU Memory Lab) https://www.cmu.edu/dietrich/psychology/memorylab/publications/10.1.1.646.3474.pdf
A reader of an instruction manual remembers the written steps better than a cluttered diagram because the diagram was too small and hard to read. (CMU Memory Lab) https://www.cmu.edu/dietrich/psychology/memorylab/publications/10.1.1.646.3474.pdf
A student remembers a written chart's exact numbers better than a picture because they needed the precise figures for a math problem, not a general impression. (CMU Memory Lab) https://www.cmu.edu/dietrich/psychology/memorylab/publications/10.1.1.646.3474.pdf
A driver remembers a written road sign better than a picture based one because the picture symbol was unfamiliar and used only in that one region. (CMU Memory Lab) https://www.cmu.edu/dietrich/psychology/memorylab/publications/10.1.1.646.3474.pdf
A shopper remembers a written price tag better than a picture of the product because the price was the only detail relevant to their decision. (CMU Memory Lab) https://www.cmu.edu/dietrich/psychology/memorylab/publications/10.1.1.646.3474.pdf
A child remembers the plain written words in a story better than the illustrations because a teacher had them practice reading the words aloud repeatedly. (CMU Memory Lab) https://www.cmu.edu/dietrich/psychology/memorylab/publications/10.1.1.646.3474.pdf
A researcher finds no memory advantage for pictures when participants are asked to judge abstract physical properties rather than freely recall the images. (CMU Memory Lab) https://www.cmu.edu/dietrich/psychology/memorylab/publications/10.1.1.646.3474.pdf
An employee remembers a coworker's written job title better than their photo because they had never actually met that coworker in person. (CMU Memory Lab) https://www.cmu.edu/dietrich/psychology/memorylab/publications/10.1.1.646.3474.pdf
A tourist remembers the written name of a landmark better than the postcard picture because the picture looked similar to several other landmarks they had seen that trip. (CMU Memory Lab) https://www.cmu.edu/dietrich/psychology/memorylab/publications/10.1.1.646.3474.pdf
A student remembers a written article's statistics better than an infographic because the infographic left out several key numbers the article included. (CMU Memory Lab) https://www.cmu.edu/dietrich/psychology/memorylab/publications/10.1.1.646.3474.pdf
A diner remembers a written menu description better than a photo of the dish because the photo did not match what was actually served. (CMU Memory Lab) https://www.cmu.edu/dietrich/psychology/memorylab/publications/10.1.1.646.3474.pdf

column3: information related to “me” is remembered and valued more.
column4:
1. You remember feedback about you most. 
2. You recall facts tied to your hobby. 
3. You notice your name in noise. 
4. Personalized advice sticks more.  
5. You remember your role in events best.

A person remembers a list of personality traits far better when asked whether each trait describes themselves compared to when asked whether each trait simply looks a certain way on the page. (Rogers, Kuiper, & Kirker, 1977) https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/909043/
A patient remembers a doctor's warning about a disease far more vividly once they realize the disease runs in their own family. (Rogers, Kuiper, & Kirker, 1977) https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/909043/
A student in a psychology class remembers information about a health condition more vividly right after learning they might have symptoms of it themselves. (Rogers, Kuiper, & Kirker, 1977) https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/909043/
A shopper remembers an ad far better when the actor in it resembles their own age and background compared to an unrelated actor. (Symons & Johnson, 1997) https://www.researchgate.net/publication/14081070_The_Self-Reference_Effect_in_Memory_A_Meta-Analysis
An employee remembers a policy change at work far better once they realize it directly affects their own paycheck. (Rogers, Kuiper, & Kirker, 1977) https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/909043/
A voter remembers a proposed tax law far better once they calculate exactly how it will affect their own household budget. (Symons & Johnson, 1997) https://www.researchgate.net/publication/14081070_The_Self-Reference_Effect_in_Memory_A_Meta-Analysis
A student remembers a list of career descriptions far better when rating how well each one describes their own future goals than when just reading the list. (Rogers, Kuiper, & Kirker, 1977) https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/909043/
A social media user remembers a post far better once they realize it mentions their own hometown. (Symons & Johnson, 1997) https://www.researchgate.net/publication/14081070_The_Self-Reference_Effect_in_Memory_A_Meta-Analysis
A patient remembers a nutrition pamphlet far better once a nurse points out that a listed risk factor applies specifically to the patient's own age group. (Rogers, Kuiper, & Kirker, 1977) https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/909043/
A person remembers a news story about a scam far better once they realize the scam targets people in their own profession. (Symons & Johnson, 1997) https://www.researchgate.net/publication/14081070_The_Self-Reference_Effect_in_Memory_A_Meta-Analysis
A student remembers a list of vocabulary words far better after being asked to use each word in a sentence about their own life than after simply copying the words. (Rogers, Kuiper, & Kirker, 1977) https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/909043/
A juror remembers a piece of testimony far better once they realize it closely resembles something that happened to them personally. (Symons & Johnson, 1997) https://www.researchgate.net/publication/14081070_The_Self-Reference_Effect_in_Memory_A_Meta-Analysis
A shopper remembers a product review far better once they notice the reviewer shares their exact same skin type or condition. (Symons & Johnson, 1997) https://www.researchgate.net/publication/14081070_The_Self-Reference_Effect_in_Memory_A_Meta-Analysis
A researcher finds that participants recall trait adjectives far better when asked if the trait applies to themselves than when asked structural or phonemic questions about the same words. (Rogers, Kuiper, & Kirker, 1977) https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/909043/
A person remembers a workplace safety statistic far better once they realize it applies directly to their own job title. (Symons & Johnson, 1997) https://www.researchgate.net/publication/14081070_The_Self-Reference_Effect_in_Memory_A_Meta-Analysis
A student remembers a historical event far better after being asked to imagine how they personally would have reacted if they had lived through it. (Rogers, Kuiper, & Kirker, 1977) https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/909043/
A patient remembers a list of medication side effects far better once a pharmacist points out which one matches a symptom the patient already has. (Rogers, Kuiper, & Kirker, 1977) https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/909043/
A person remembers a financial planning seminar far better once the speaker uses an example involving their exact same salary range. (Symons & Johnson, 1997) https://www.researchgate.net/publication/14081070_The_Self-Reference_Effect_in_Memory_A_Meta-Analysis
An employee remembers feedback from a performance review far better than general company announcements because the feedback was about their own specific work. (Rogers, Kuiper, & Kirker, 1977) https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/909043/
A student remembers an example problem in math class far better after the teacher uses the student's own name and hobby in the word problem. (Rogers, Kuiper, & Kirker, 1977) https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/909043/
column5:
1. You remember impersonal info because it’s meaningful. 
2. You follow objective priorities over personal interest. 
3. You recall others’ details well too. 
4. You separate ego from judging evidence. 
5. Relevance doesn’t change what’s true.


A person remembers a list of personality traits equally well whether or not they are asked to relate the traits to themselves, because they were told the list would be tested with a strict word for word quiz that rewarded rote memorization instead. (Rogers, Kuiper, & Kirker, 1977) https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/909043/
A patient forgets a doctor's warning about a disease even after learning it runs in their family, because the appointment was rushed and the warning was never repeated or written down. (Rogers, Kuiper, & Kirker, 1977) https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/909043/
A shopper remembers an unrelated actor in an ad just as well as a relatable one because the ad's jingle was catchy enough to be memorable on its own. (Symons & Johnson, 1997) https://www.researchgate.net/publication/14081070_The_Self-Reference_Effect_in_Memory_A_Meta-Analysis
An employee forgets a policy change that affects their own paycheck because the announcement email was buried among dozens of other unread messages. (Rogers, Kuiper, & Kirker, 1977) https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/909043/
A voter forgets the details of a tax law that affects their own budget because the news coverage of it was brief and never followed up on. (Symons & Johnson, 1997) https://www.researchgate.net/publication/14081070_The_Self-Reference_Effect_in_Memory_A_Meta-Analysis
A student remembers a career description just as well whether or not it relates to their own goals, because all the descriptions were tied to a mandatory exam question. (Rogers, Kuiper, & Kirker, 1977) https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/909043/
A social media user scrolls past a post mentioning their hometown without remembering it later because they were distracted and did not actually read the caption. (Symons & Johnson, 1997) https://www.researchgate.net/publication/14081070_The_Self-Reference_Effect_in_Memory_A_Meta-Analysis
A patient forgets a risk factor that applies to their age group because the nurse mentioned it only once in passing without any follow up material. (Rogers, Kuiper, & Kirker, 1977) https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/909043/
A person remembers a scam warning that targets a different profession than their own just as well, because the story involved a large enough dollar amount to be memorable regardless. (Symons & Johnson, 1997) https://www.researchgate.net/publication/14081070_The_Self-Reference_Effect_in_Memory_A_Meta-Analysis
A student remembers vocabulary words equally well whether or not they use them in personal sentences, because the words were also set to music in a repeated classroom chant. (Rogers, Kuiper, & Kirker, 1977) https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/909043/
A juror forgets testimony that resembled something personal to them because the testimony was given late in a long trial when attention had already faded. (Symons & Johnson, 1997) https://www.researchgate.net/publication/14081070_The_Self-Reference_Effect_in_Memory_A_Meta-Analysis
A shopper forgets a product review from someone with their same skin type because the review was poorly written and hard to follow. (Symons & Johnson, 1997) https://www.researchgate.net/publication/14081070_The_Self-Reference_Effect_in_Memory_A_Meta-Analysis
A participant recalls trait adjectives equally well across self-reference and semantic tasks once both tasks require the same amount of elaborate thinking about the word's meaning. (Rogers, Kuiper, & Kirker, 1977) https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/909043/
A person forgets a safety statistic relevant to their job because it was presented in a mandatory training video they treated as background noise. (Symons & Johnson, 1997) https://www.researchgate.net/publication/14081070_The_Self-Reference_Effect_in_Memory_A_Meta-Analysis
A student forgets a historical event even after imagining their own reaction to it, because the imagining exercise was rushed and never discussed again. (Rogers, Kuiper, & Kirker, 1977) https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/909043/
A patient forgets a medication side effect that matches their own symptom because the pharmacist read the list too quickly during a busy pickup. (Rogers, Kuiper, & Kirker, 1977) https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/909043/
A person forgets details from a financial seminar that matched their own salary range because the seminar ran two hours past its scheduled time and fatigue set in. (Symons & Johnson, 1997) https://www.researchgate.net/publication/14081070_The_Self-Reference_Effect_in_Memory_A_Meta-Analysis
An employee forgets personal feedback from a performance review because it was delivered verbally with no written summary to refer back to later. (Rogers, Kuiper, & Kirker, 1977) https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/909043/
A student forgets a math word problem that used their own name because the underlying math concept itself was never properly explained. (Rogers, Kuiper, & Kirker, 1977) https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/909043/
A person remembers a general safety statistic just as well whether or not it applies to their own job, because their employer required a signed quiz on it every single month. (Symons & Johnson, 1997) https://www.researchgate.net/publication/14081070_The_Self-Reference_Effect_in_Memory_A_Meta-Analysis

column3: negative events/information weigh more than positive ones.
column4:
1. One insult outweighs five compliments. 
2. A bad review dominates your impression. 
3. You replay one mistake all day. 
4. Threats grab attention faster than opportunities. 
5. Failures feel more memorable than wins.


A worker who receives nine pieces of positive feedback and one piece of criticism in a performance review spends the whole evening dwelling only on the criticism. (Baumeister, Bratslavsky, Finkenauer, & Vohs, 2001) https://research.vu.nl/en/publications/bad-is-stronger-than-good-2/
A shopper reading online reviews weighs a single one star complaint far more heavily than a dozen five star reviews for the same product. (Baumeister, Bratslavsky, Finkenauer, & Vohs, 2001) https://research.vu.nl/en/publications/bad-is-stronger-than-good-2/
A voter remembers a single scandal about a candidate far more vividly than years of that candidate's accomplishments. (Baumeister, Bratslavsky, Finkenauer, & Vohs, 2001) https://research.vu.nl/en/publications/bad-is-stronger-than-good-2/
An infant reacts more strongly and pays closer attention to an angry facial expression than to a happy one shown for the same length of time. (Vaish, Grossmann, & Woodward, 2008) https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC3652533/
A news outlet finds that headlines about disasters and scandals get far more clicks than headlines about positive community events. (Baumeister, Bratslavsky, Finkenauer, & Vohs, 2001) https://research.vu.nl/en/publications/bad-is-stronger-than-good-2/
A couple's relationship satisfaction is predicted far more strongly by their negative interactions than by their positive ones. (Baumeister, Bratslavsky, Finkenauer, & Vohs, 2001) https://research.vu.nl/en/publications/bad-is-stronger-than-good-2/
A student who gets one harsh comment on an essay along with several compliments only remembers the harsh comment a week later. (Baumeister, Bratslavsky, Finkenauer, & Vohs, 2001) https://research.vu.nl/en/publications/bad-is-stronger-than-good-2/
An investor reacts far more strongly to a stock losing five percent in a day than to it gaining the same five percent. (Baumeister, Bratslavsky, Finkenauer, & Vohs, 2001) https://research.vu.nl/en/publications/bad-is-stronger-than-good-2/
A toddler learns to avoid touching a hot stove after just one painful experience, much faster than they learn to seek out a pleasant new toy. (Vaish, Grossmann, & Woodward, 2008) https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC3652533/
A restaurant owner finds that one bad review spreads among friends and family far faster than glowing praise about the same meal. (Baumeister, Bratslavsky, Finkenauer, & Vohs, 2001) https://research.vu.nl/en/publications/bad-is-stronger-than-good-2/
A job candidate's single awkward moment in an interview sticks in the interviewer's mind far longer than several strong answers given the same day. (Baumeister, Bratslavsky, Finkenauer, & Vohs, 2001) https://research.vu.nl/en/publications/bad-is-stronger-than-good-2/
A social media user remembers one rude comment on a post far more vividly than dozens of kind comments left on the same post. (Baumeister, Bratslavsky, Finkenauer, & Vohs, 2001) https://research.vu.nl/en/publications/bad-is-stronger-than-good-2/
A patient remembers a single frightening statistic about a surgery's risks far more vividly than the doctor's reassurance about its high success rate. (Baumeister, Bratslavsky, Finkenauer, & Vohs, 2001) https://research.vu.nl/en/publications/bad-is-stronger-than-good-2/
A baby shows a stronger and faster physical startle response to a sudden loud noise than any equally sudden pleasant sound. (Vaish, Grossmann, & Woodward, 2008) https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC3652533/
A manager's memory of a single missed deadline overshadows an employee's long track record of finishing projects early. (Baumeister, Bratslavsky, Finkenauer, & Vohs, 2001) https://research.vu.nl/en/publications/bad-is-stronger-than-good-2/
A traveler remembers one unpleasant airport delay far more vividly than an entire smooth, enjoyable vacation. (Baumeister, Bratslavsky, Finkenauer, & Vohs, 2001) https://research.vu.nl/en/publications/bad-is-stronger-than-good-2/
A teacher notices that a single disruptive student in class draws far more of their attention and memory than an entire row of well behaved students. (Baumeister, Bratslavsky, Finkenauer, & Vohs, 2001) https://research.vu.nl/en/publications/bad-is-stronger-than-good-2/
A person forms a negative first impression of a new coworker after one awkward interaction and it takes many positive interactions afterward to change that impression. (Baumeister, Bratslavsky, Finkenauer, & Vohs, 2001) https://research.vu.nl/en/publications/bad-is-stronger-than-good-2/
A reader of a movie review site weighs the few scathing reviews far more heavily in their decision than the many favorable ones. (Baumeister, Bratslavsky, Finkenauer, & Vohs, 2001) https://research.vu.nl/en/publications/bad-is-stronger-than-good-2/
A person recalling their wedding day remembers the one thing that went wrong far more vividly than the dozens of things that went right. (Baumeister, Bratslavsky, Finkenauer, & Vohs, 2001) https://research.vu.nl/en/publications/bad-is-stronger-than-good-2/
column5:
1. You weigh evidence proportionally. 
2. You keep a “wins list” to balance. 3. You savor positives deliberately. 
4. You reframe mistakes as learning data. 
5. Small negatives don’t hijack your attention.

A student who gets a single harsh comment on an essay alongside several compliments moves on quickly and focuses on making the suggested revision rather than dwelling on the criticism. (Rethinking the Negativity Bias, 2019) https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC6132407/
A shopper reading reviews gives roughly equal weight to a single one star complaint and a single five star review because both were written by verified buyers with photos attached. (Rethinking the Negativity Bias, 2019) https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC6132407/
A voter's opinion of a candidate improves steadily over years of strong accomplishments even after one early scandal, showing repeated good news can outweigh a single bad event over time. (Rethinking the Negativity Bias, 2019) https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC6132407/
A toddler shows equal attention to a happy and an angry face when both expressions are shown by a stranger with a neutral tone of voice. (Vaish, Grossmann, & Woodward, 2008) https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC3652533/
A news outlet finds that a heartwarming rescue story outperforms a disaster headline in shares that week because of an unusually inspiring twist. (Rethinking the Negativity Bias, 2019) https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC6132407/
A couple's relationship satisfaction is predicted just as strongly by their frequent positive interactions as by their occasional negative ones, according to one study that found the ratio, not just the negative events, mattered most. (Rethinking the Negativity Bias, 2019) https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC6132407/
An investor reacts just as strongly to a stock gaining five percent as losing it, because the investor had set an automatic alert for either five percent move regardless of direction. (Rethinking the Negativity Bias, 2019) https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC6132407/
A restaurant owner finds that a single glowing review from a well known food critic spreads just as fast as a bad review from an anonymous customer. (Rethinking the Negativity Bias, 2019) https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC6132407/
A job candidate's one awkward moment is quickly forgotten by an interviewer who was specifically trained to focus only on structured scorecard answers. (Rethinking the Negativity Bias, 2019) https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC6132407/
A social media user remembers a especially funny kind comment just as vividly as a rude one because the kind comment was pinned to the top of the post. (Rethinking the Negativity Bias, 2019) https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC6132407/
A patient remembers a doctor's reassurance about a surgery's high success rate just as clearly as the risk statistic because the doctor repeated the success rate three times during the visit. (Rethinking the Negativity Bias, 2019) https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC6132407/
A manager remembers an employee's early finished projects just as clearly as a later missed deadline because the manager kept a written log of both throughout the year. (Rethinking the Negativity Bias, 2019) https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC6132407/
A traveler remembers an entire smooth vacation fondly, with the one delay barely registering, because the delay was brief and quickly resolved with a free upgrade. (Rethinking the Negativity Bias, 2019) https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC6132407/
A teacher remembers a quiet, well behaved student just as clearly as a disruptive one because the well behaved student won a schoolwide award that year. (Rethinking the Negativity Bias, 2019) https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC6132407/
A person's first impression of a new coworker stays positive despite one awkward interaction, since the coworker immediately apologized and followed up warmly. (Rethinking the Negativity Bias, 2019) https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC6132407/
A reader of a movie review site weighs many glowing reviews more heavily than a couple of scathing ones once they notice the negative reviews came from bots. (Rethinking the Negativity Bias, 2019) https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC6132407/
A person recalling their wedding day remembers the entire event as joyful and barely thinks about the one minor mishap, since it was fixed within minutes and no guests even noticed. (Rethinking the Negativity Bias, 2019) https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC6132407/
An infant shows a stronger response to an unusually loud happy laugh than to a quiet angry mutter, since volume rather than emotional tone drove the reaction in that instance. (Vaish, Grossmann, & Woodward, 2008) https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC3652533/
A worker who receives one piece of criticism forgets it by the next morning because their manager immediately paired it with a specific, actionable plan to fix it. (Rethinking the Negativity Bias, 2019) https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC6132407/
A student remembers positive and negative feedback about equally well because both were delivered in the exact same calm, matter of fact tone during a routine check in. (Rethinking the Negativity Bias, 2019) https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC6132407/

column3: the first number/idea you see becomes a reference point that biases later judgments.
column4:
1. Original price makes a sale look amazing. 
2. First trials in an experiment that were great make the following fails seem terrible 
3. Starting bid shapes the final price. 
4. First impression anchors your opinion of someone. 
5. Suggested donation sets what feels “normal.”

A jacket is labeled “$300” then discounted to $180, and it feels “cheap” because you anchored on $300.
You hear someone suggest “around 2 hours,” and your estimate stays near 2 hours even after new info.
The first salary number mentioned in negotiation pulls your counteroffer toward it.
After seeing a $2,000 phone, a $1,200 phone feels “reasonable” (anchored on the first price).
A random “spin-the-wheel” number influences how many countries you guess are in Africa.


A shopper sees a jacket marked down from two hundred dollars to eighty dollars and feels like eighty dollars is a great deal, even though the two hundred dollar price was never real. (Tversky & Kahneman, 1974) https://bear.warrington.ufl.edu/brenner/mar7588/Papers/tversky-kahneman-science-1974.pdf
A person spins a wheel that lands on a random high number and then gives a much higher guess for an unrelated question about world statistics than someone who saw the wheel land on a low number. (Tversky & Kahneman, 1974) https://bear.warrington.ufl.edu/brenner/mar7588/Papers/tversky-kahneman-science-1974.pdf
A home buyer's opinion of a fair price for a house is swayed by the first listing price they saw, even after learning that price was set unusually high. (Tversky & Kahneman, 1974) https://bear.warrington.ufl.edu/brenner/mar7588/Papers/tversky-kahneman-science-1974.pdf
A salary negotiation ends up close to the first number mentioned by either side, regardless of what the job is actually worth in the market. (Tversky & Kahneman, 1974) https://bear.warrington.ufl.edu/brenner/mar7588/Papers/tversky-kahneman-science-1974.pdf
A juror's estimate of appropriate damages in a lawsuit is swayed by the very first dollar amount a lawyer mentions in opening statements. (Tversky & Kahneman, 1974) https://bear.warrington.ufl.edu/brenner/mar7588/Papers/tversky-kahneman-science-1974.pdf
A student guessing the population of a foreign country gives a higher answer after being told a clearly made up large number beforehand than after being told a small one. (Tversky & Kahneman, 1974) https://bear.warrington.ufl.edu/brenner/mar7588/Papers/tversky-kahneman-science-1974.pdf
A car buyer's final offer ends up much closer to the dealer's inflated sticker price than to the car's actual resale value. (Tversky & Kahneman, 1974) https://bear.warrington.ufl.edu/brenner/mar7588/Papers/tversky-kahneman-science-1974.pdf
A doctor's diagnosis is swayed by the very first symptom a patient happens to mention, even after later symptoms suggest something different. (Tversky & Kahneman, 1974) https://bear.warrington.ufl.edu/brenner/mar7588/Papers/tversky-kahneman-science-1974.pdf
A restaurant menu lists one extremely expensive dish at the top, making the other prices on the menu feel more reasonable by comparison. (Tversky & Kahneman, 1974) https://bear.warrington.ufl.edu/brenner/mar7588/Papers/tversky-kahneman-science-1974.pdf

A charity's suggested donation amounts on a form influence how much people actually give, even when the suggested amounts are arbitrary. (Tversky & Kahneman, 1974) https://bear.warrington.ufl.edu/brenner/mar7588/Papers/tversky-kahneman-science-1974.pdf

The original price is what makes the sale price feel cheap.
Was five pounds, now three — the five sets what three feels like.
Marked down from a number nobody was ever going to pay.
A jacket originally priced at two hundred and fifty dollars is on sale for one hundred and ninety, and the original price is what makes the saving feel real.
A coat was originally priced at four hundred dollars and is now on sale for two hundred and fifty; shoppers judge the discount against the original price rather than against what the coat is worth.
A store prints the original price beside the sale price, and the sale price only feels cheap because the original is sitting next to it.
A sofa marked down from nine hundred pounds to six hundred feels like a bargain because the nine hundred was the first number seen.
An online listing shows a struck-through recommended retail price above the current price, so the current price feels reasonable by comparison.
A retailer raises the original price shortly before a sale so that the reduced price reads as a larger saving than it is.
A supermarket shelf label reading 'was five pounds, now three pounds' sets what three pounds feels like, whatever the item normally sells for.
A shopper who sees a laptop originally priced at fifteen hundred dollars now offered at eleven hundred judges the deal against the original price rather than against competing laptops.
A ticket site displays a higher standard fare beside the offer fare so that the offer reads as value.
A furniture shop runs a permanent closing-down sale, keeping a high original price on display so every price beneath it looks discounted.
A shopper feels a two hundred dollar pair of boots reduced to one hundred and forty is a good buy without ever asking what the boots are worth.
An estate agent lists a house above what it will sell for, so every later offer is judged against the asking price rather than the market.

column3: thinking in “nominal” money (numbers) instead of real value (inflation/purchasing power).
column4:
1. Feeling richer after a raise that doesn’t beat inflation. 
2. Preferring $110 today over $100 yesterday without inflation context. 
3. Thinking prices “went up” but wages did too. 
4. Saving cash long-term ignoring inflation erosion. 
5. Comparing salaries across years without adjusting inflation.

A worker feels thrilled about a three percent raise during a year when inflation is running at five percent, even though their real buying power actually dropped. (Shafir, Diamond, & Tversky, 1997) https://collaborate.princeton.edu/en/publications/money-illusion-2/
A homeowner refuses to sell a house for less than they originally paid for it, even though inflation means that price now represents a real loss. (Shafir, Diamond, & Tversky, 1997) https://collaborate.princeton.edu/en/publications/money-illusion-2/
An employee feels a pay freeze during high inflation is fair, not realizing it amounts to a real pay cut once rising prices are factored in. (Shafir, Diamond, & Tversky, 1997) https://collaborate.princeton.edu/en/publications/money-illusion-2/
A retiree feels financially secure seeing their savings account balance grow slowly, without accounting for how inflation is eroding its actual purchasing power. (Shafir, Diamond, & Tversky, 1997) https://collaborate.princeton.edu/en/publications/money-illusion-2/
A person feels richer after their salary doubles over ten years, without factoring in that prices for everything they buy also roughly doubled over the same period. (Shafir, Diamond, & Tversky, 1997) https://collaborate.princeton.edu/en/publications/money-illusion-2/
A landlord feels a rent increase matching inflation is unfair to tenants, treating the nominal dollar increase as a real gain for themselves. (Shafir, Diamond, & Tversky, 1997) https://collaborate.princeton.edu/en/publications/money-illusion-2/
A shopper feels prices have "gone up a lot" this year, focusing on nominal dollar figures rather than comparing the increase to their own rising wages. (Shafir, Diamond, & Tversky, 1997) https://collaborate.princeton.edu/en/publications/money-illusion-2/
A business owner is reluctant to cut nominal wages during a downturn even when it would preserve real wages better than a wage freeze during inflation would. (Shafir, Diamond, & Tversky, 1997) https://collaborate.princeton.edu/en/publications/money-illusion-2/
A person feels good about winning a "ten thousand dollar" prize today without adjusting for the fact that the same nominal amount would have been worth far more decades ago. (Shafir, Diamond, & Tversky, 1997) https://collaborate.princeton.edu/en/publications/money-illusion-2/
An employee negotiating a raise focuses on the dollar figure of the increase rather than whether it actually keeps pace with the cost of living. (Shafir, Diamond, & Tversky, 1997) https://collaborate.princeton.edu/en/publications/money-illusion-2/
A saver feels good about earning two percent interest on a savings account during a year when inflation runs at four percent, not realizing their money is actually losing value. (Shafir, Diamond, & Tversky, 1997) https://collaborate.princeton.edu/en/publications/money-illusion-2/
A worker perceives a job offering a higher nominal salary in an expensive city as a better deal than a lower nominal salary in a cheap city, without adjusting for cost of living. (Shafir, Diamond, & Tversky, 1997) https://collaborate.princeton.edu/en/publications/money-illusion-2/
A shareholder feels satisfied when a stock's nominal price rises, without checking whether the gain actually outpaced inflation over that period. (Shafir, Diamond, & Tversky, 1997) https://collaborate.princeton.edu/en/publications/money-illusion-2/
A parent tells their child that a dollar today "buys just as much" as a dollar did decades ago, ignoring decades of inflation. (Shafir, Diamond, & Tversky, 1997) https://collaborate.princeton.edu/en/publications/money-illusion-2/
A tenant is more upset by a landlord raising rent by fifty dollars than by the landlord raising rent by five percent, even when the dollar amounts are identical. (Shafir, Diamond, & Tversky, 1997) https://collaborate.princeton.edu/en/publications/money-illusion-2/
A person feels a two dollar increase in a coffee's price is outrageous, without adjusting the comparison for how much wages have also risen since they first started buying that coffee. (Shafir, Diamond, & Tversky, 1997) https://collaborate.princeton.edu/en/publications/money-illusion-2/
An employer is more comfortable freezing nominal wages during high inflation than explicitly cutting wages during low inflation, even when the second option is actually a smaller real pay cut. (Shafir, Diamond, & Tversky, 1997) https://collaborate.princeton.edu/en/publications/money-illusion-2/
A retiree feels their pension is generous because the nominal monthly check is larger than it was twenty years ago, without comparing it to today's higher cost of living. (Shafir, Diamond, & Tversky, 1997) https://collaborate.princeton.edu/en/publications/money-illusion-2/
A borrower feels relieved that their loan's dollar payments have not increased, without realizing inflation has made those fixed payments easier to afford in real terms, which they never actually notice or credit. (Shafir, Diamond, & Tversky, 1997) https://collaborate.princeton.edu/en/publications/money-illusion-2/
An investor compares two countries' stock market returns using only nominal percentage gains, without adjusting either country's number for its own inflation rate. (Shafir, Diamond, & Tversky, 1997) https://collaborate.princeton.edu/en/publications/money-illusion-2/
column5:
1. You adjust for inflation (real terms). 
2. You compare purchasing power (what it buys). 
3. You use “real” returns not nominal returns. 
4. You check cost-of-living differences. 
5. You track inflation rates alongside pay/prices.

An economist calculates a worker's real wage change by subtracting the inflation rate from the nominal raise, correctly concluding the three percent raise was actually a pay cut. (Shafir, Diamond, & Tversky, 1997) https://collaborate.princeton.edu/en/publications/money-illusion-2/
A homeowner sells their house for less than they paid, having calculated that after accounting for inflation, the sale still represents a real financial gain. (Shafir, Diamond, & Tversky, 1997) https://collaborate.princeton.edu/en/publications/money-illusion-2/
A financial advisor recommends a client accept a nominal wage cut during a period of falling prices, correctly explaining that it preserves the client's real purchasing power. (Shafir, Diamond, & Tversky, 1997) https://collaborate.princeton.edu/en/publications/money-illusion-2/
A retiree tracks their savings account's real return by comparing the interest rate to the inflation rate each year, correctly recognizing when they are losing purchasing power. (Shafir, Diamond, & Tversky, 1997) https://collaborate.princeton.edu/en/publications/money-illusion-2/
A person calculates that their salary doubling over ten years resulted in no real gain at all, since prices also roughly doubled over the same period. (Shafir, Diamond, & Tversky, 1997) https://collaborate.princeton.edu/en/publications/money-illusion-2/
A tenant calculates that a landlord's rent increase exactly matches inflation and correctly concludes it represents no real change in the landlord's income. (Shafir, Diamond, & Tversky, 1997) https://collaborate.princeton.edu/en/publications/money-illusion-2/
A shopper compares this year's grocery prices to last year's using an official inflation index, correctly separating real price increases from ones that just match inflation. (Shafir, Diamond, & Tversky, 1997) https://collaborate.princeton.edu/en/publications/money-illusion-2/
A worker calculates that a job offering a higher nominal salary in an expensive city is actually a worse deal once local cost of living is factored in. (Shafir, Diamond, & Tversky, 1997) https://collaborate.princeton.edu/en/publications/money-illusion-2/
A shareholder checks whether a stock's nominal gain outpaced inflation before deciding whether the investment was actually profitable in real terms. (Shafir, Diamond, & Tversky, 1997) https://collaborate.princeton.edu/en/publications/money-illusion-2/
A parent correctly explains to their child that a dollar today buys far less than a dollar did decades ago, citing decades of documented inflation. (Shafir, Diamond, & Tversky, 1997) https://collaborate.princeton.edu/en/publications/money-illusion-2/
A tenant reacts the same way to a fifty dollar rent increase and an equivalent five percent increase, correctly recognizing they represent the same real cost. (Shafir, Diamond, & Tversky, 1997) https://collaborate.princeton.edu/en/publications/money-illusion-2/
A person calculates that a two dollar coffee price increase is actually smaller in real terms than the last increase, since their own wages rose by a larger percentage in the meantime. (Shafir, Diamond, & Tversky, 1997) https://collaborate.princeton.edu/en/publications/money-illusion-2/
An employer explicitly cuts nominal wages during low inflation rather than freezing them, having calculated it results in a smaller real pay cut for employees overall. (Shafir, Diamond, & Tversky, 1997) https://collaborate.princeton.edu/en/publications/money-illusion-2/
A retiree calculates that their larger nominal pension check actually buys less than their smaller check did twenty years ago, once adjusted for the cost of living. (Shafir, Diamond, & Tversky, 1997) https://collaborate.princeton.edu/en/publications/money-illusion-2/
A borrower explicitly credits inflation for making their fixed loan payments easier to afford over time, correctly separating nominal and real value. (Shafir, Diamond, & Tversky, 1997) https://collaborate.princeton.edu/en/publications/money-illusion-2/
An investor compares two countries' stock returns only after adjusting each one for that country's own inflation rate, correctly ranking the real performance. (Shafir, Diamond, & Tversky, 1997) https://collaborate.princeton.edu/en/publications/money-illusion-2/
A business owner correctly explains to employees that a wage freeze during high inflation is functionally identical to an explicit pay cut, and budgets accordingly. (Shafir, Diamond, & Tversky, 1997) https://collaborate.princeton.edu/en/publications/money-illusion-2/
A shopper calculates that despite winning a ten thousand dollar prize today, the equivalent prize decades ago would have been worth far more in real terms. (Shafir, Diamond, & Tversky, 1997) https://collaborate.princeton.edu/en/publications/money-illusion-2/
An employee negotiating a raise explicitly ties the requested percentage to the current inflation rate, ensuring the raise preserves real purchasing power. (Shafir, Diamond, & Tversky, 1997) https://collaborate.princeton.edu/en/publications/money-illusion-2/
A landlord calculates a rent increase strictly based on the real cost of maintaining the property after inflation, rather than treating the nominal dollar increase as extra profit. (Shafir, Diamond, & Tversky, 1997) https://collaborate.princeton.edu/en/publications/money-illusion-2/

column3: judging something as better/more true because it “fits” with what you already think/feel. favoring information that supports your existing beliefs and ignoring conflicting evidence.
column4:
1. A claim feels true because it matches your worldview. 
2. You trust a theory because it aligns with your values. 
3. You accept a stereotype because it “seems right.” 
4. You prefer arguments that match your mood. 
5. You rate a story believable because it’s consistent with your expectations.
1. Only reading articles that agree with you. 
2. Noticing “proof” for your opinion but dismissing counter-data. 
3. Remembering wins and forgetting misses.
 4. Interpreting mixed results as supportive. 
5. Following social media accounts that reinforce your view.


A person who believes vaccines are dangerous only reads articles that support that view and skips over articles citing safety data. (Nickerson, 1998) https://journals.sagepub.com/doi/10.1037/1089-2680.2.2.175
A manager who already thinks a new hire is a poor fit notices every small mistake they make while overlooking their successes. (ScienceDirect Topics, Confirmation Bias) https://www.sciencedirect.com/topics/psychology/confirmation-bias
A sports fan who is convinced the referee is biased against their team only remembers the calls that went against them. (Britannica, Confirmation Bias) https://www.britannica.com/science/confirmation-bias
A scientist who expects an experiment to succeed unconsciously interprets ambiguous data as supporting their hypothesis. (Nickerson, 1998) https://pages.ucsd.edu/~mckenzie/nickersonConfirmationBias.pdf

A picky eater who assumes a new food will taste bad asks only questions likely to confirm it is unappealing. (ScienceDirect Topics, Confirmation Bias) https://www.sciencedirect.com/topics/psychology/confirmation-bias
A juror who forms an early impression of a defendant's guilt pays closer attention to testimony that supports that belief. (Nickerson, 1998) https://journals.sagepub.com/doi/10.1037/1089-2680.2.2.175
A social media user only follows accounts that agree with their political views, reinforcing what they already believe. (Survey on Echo Chambers on Social Media, 2021) https://arxiv.org/pdf/2112.05084
A doctor who suspects a patient has a certain illness orders tests that would confirm it while skipping tests that might rule it out. (Nickerson, 1998) https://pages.ucsd.edu/~mckenzie/nickersonConfirmationBias.pdf
A shopper who believes a certain brand is superior only reads five-star reviews and skips the negative ones. (Britannica, Confirmation Bias) https://www.britannica.com/science/confirmation-bias
An investor who believes a stock will rise seeks out only bullish analyst opinions and dismisses bearish warnings. (Nickerson, 1998) https://journals.sagepub.com/doi/10.1037/1089-2680.2.2.175
A teacher who expects a student to struggle interprets an average test score as proof of that struggle rather than progress. (ScienceDirect Topics, Confirmation Bias) https://www.sciencedirect.com/topics/psychology/confirmation-bias

column3: noticing and interpreting information in ways that match your expectations (what you “look for” is what you “see”).
column4:
1. Expect rudeness → you notice neutral comments as rude. 
2. Think you’re bad at math → notice mistakes more than successes. 
3. Believe a class is boring → notice every dull moment. 
4. Assume a place is unsafe → focus on suspicious cues. 
5. Expect a friend to ignore you → interpret late replies as rejection.

column3: a researcher/observer’s expectations influence what they notice and record.
column4:
1. Teacher expects a student to do poorly → grades harsher. 
2. Coach expects laziness → notices only low effort. 
3. Doctor expects anxiety → overlooks physical causes. 
4. Judge expects arrogance → interprets confidence as disrespect. 
5. Researcher expects effect → records ambiguous data as positive.

Psychology students told their lab rats were bred "maze-bright" got noticeably better maze results than students told their rats were "maze-dull," even though all rats were identical. (Rosenthal & Fode, 1963) https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Observer_bias
A horse named Clever Hans appeared to solve math problems, but was actually just picking up on unconscious cues from his trainer's body language. (Grokipedia, Observer-Expectancy Effect) https://grokipedia.com/page/Observer-expectancy_effect
A teacher who is told a student is "gifted" unconsciously gives that student more encouragement, and the student's performance improves as a result. (Quiet Storm Solutions, Rosenthal and Maze Smart Rats) https://www.quietstorm.net/robert-rosenthal-and-maze-smart-rats/

A veterinary student told an animal is "calm" handles it more gently, causing the animal to actually behave more calmly during the exam. (Grokipedia, Observer-Expectancy Effect) https://grokipedia.com/page/Observer-expectancy_effect

A supervisor who is told a new employee has "leadership potential" unconsciously offers that employee more guidance, leading to visibly stronger performance. (Robert Rosenthal, "What You Expect Is What You Get") https://homepages.gac.edu/~jwotton2/PSY225/rosenthal66.pdf
A researcher grading essays who is told certain students are "high achievers" unconsciously scores their ambiguous answers more generously. (Practical Psychology, Experimenter Bias) https://practicalpie.com/experimenter-bias/
A psychic's assistant unconsciously feeds subtle cues to a psychic during a demonstration, making vague guesses seem uncannily accurate. (What Is Observer Bias?) https://scales.arabpsychology.com/stats/what-is-observer-bias/
A physical therapist who expects a patient's treatment to work provides subtly more encouragement, and the patient reports feeling better as a result. (Grokipedia, Observer-Expectancy Effect) https://grokipedia.com/page/Observer-expectancy_effect
A researcher measuring reaction times unconsciously starts the stopwatch slightly earlier for participants they expect to perform well. (Practical Psychology, Experimenter Bias) https://practicalpie.com/experimenter-bias/
A zoo keeper who is told a new animal is "friendly" approaches it with relaxed body language, and the animal responds calmly in turn. (What Is Observer Bias?) https://scales.arabpsychology.com/stats/what-is-observer-bias/

A researcher conducting an unblinded drug trial unconsciously spends more encouraging time with patients receiving the actual medication. (Practical Psychology, Experimenter Bias) https://practicalpie.com/experimenter-bias/

A music teacher who expects a student to struggle unconsciously offers fewer corrections, allowing errors to go unaddressed and performance to lag. (Robert Rosenthal, "What You Expect Is What You Get") https://homepages.gac.edu/~jwotton2/PSY225/rosenthal66.pdf
A researcher rating children's drawings for creativity scores the drawings of children they were told were "artistic" more favorably. (What Is Observer Bias?) https://scales.arabpsychology.com/stats/what-is-observer-bias/

A researcher rating children's drawings for creativity does so without knowing which children were previously labeled "artistic." (What Is Observer Bias?) https://scales.arabpsychology.com/stats/what-is-observer-bias/
A lab assistant handles all rats with identical care and timing, regardless of any label assigned to their group. (Rosenthal & Fode, 1963) https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Observer_bias

column3: a type of expectancy bias where the experimenter unintentionally influences participants/outcomes.
column4:
1. Giving subtle hints to “correct” answers.
 2. Different tone/body language changes participant responses. 
3. Leading questions in an interview study. 
4. Smiling more when the “right” behavior appears.
 5. Recording borderline results as success.

A researcher who believes a new drug works designs the study without a control group, making it impossible to rule out other explanations for improvement. (Rosenthal, "What You Expect Is What You Get") https://homepages.gac.edu/~jwotton2/PSY225/rosenthal66.pdf
A scientist analyzing survey data chooses to exclude a batch of "outlier" responses that happen to be the ones contradicting their hypothesis. (Rosenthal & Fode, "Psychology of the Scientist," 1963) https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Observer_bias
A lead investigator writes the study's survey questions in a way that subtly nudges participants toward the answer the investigator expects. (Practical Psychology, Experimenter Bias) https://practicalpie.com/experimenter-bias/
A researcher who expects a teaching method to work rounds ambiguous test scores up for the experimental group and down for the control group. (What Is Observer Bias?) https://scales.arabpsychology.com/stats/what-is-observer-bias/
A scientist chooses to only publish the trial that supported their hypothesis while leaving two contradicting trials in a drawer. (Practical Psychology, Experimenter Bias) https://practicalpie.com/experimenter-bias/
An experimenter picks study participants from a group already known to be sympathetic to the hypothesis being tested. (Rosenthal, "What You Expect Is What You Get") https://homepages.gac.edu/~jwotton2/PSY225/rosenthal66.pdf
A lab director assigns the most promising-looking subjects to the treatment group instead of using true random assignment. (Rosenthal & Fode, "Psychology of the Scientist," 1963) https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Observer_bias
A researcher interprets a borderline statistical result as "significant" because it matches what they expected to find. (Practical Psychology, Experimenter Bias) https://practicalpie.com/experimenter-bias/
A scientist stops data collection early as soon as the results start looking favorable, rather than sticking to the planned sample size. (What Is Observer Bias?) https://scales.arabpsychology.com/stats/what-is-observer-bias/
A researcher coding open-ended interview responses labels ambiguous answers in the direction that supports their hypothesis. (Practical Psychology, Experimenter Bias) https://practicalpie.com/experimenter-bias/
An experimenter re-runs a failed trial multiple times but only reports the one run that produced the expected result. (Rosenthal, "What You Expect Is What You Get") https://homepages.gac.edu/~jwotton2/PSY225/rosenthal66.pdf
A researcher chooses a measurement tool known to be more sensitive to the outcome they are hoping to detect. (What Is Observer Bias?) https://scales.arabpsychology.com/stats/what-is-observer-bias/
A scientist writing up results describes a small effect size using dramatic language because it fits their expected narrative. (Practical Psychology, Experimenter Bias) https://practicalpie.com/experimenter-bias/
A lead researcher unconsciously assigns healthier-looking participants to the group receiving the new treatment. (Rosenthal & Fode, "Psychology of the Scientist," 1963) https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Observer_bias
A scientist testing a teaching app picks the classroom with the most engaged students to serve as the treatment group. (Rosenthal, "What You Expect Is What You Get") https://homepages.gac.edu/~jwotton2/PSY225/rosenthal66.pdf
An experimenter selectively re-measures a data point that seems "off" only when it goes against their hypothesis. (Practical Psychology, Experimenter Bias) https://practicalpie.com/experimenter-bias/
A researcher designs a survey scale that makes it easier for respondents to select the answer supporting the hypothesis. (What Is Observer Bias?) https://scales.arabpsychology.com/stats/what-is-observer-bias/
A scientist reviewing their own team's data applies a more lenient quality check to results that confirm their theory. (Practical Psychology, Experimenter Bias) https://practicalpie.com/experimenter-bias/
A researcher chooses to compare the treatment group's best month of data against the control group's worst month. (Rosenthal, "What You Expect Is What You Get") https://homepages.gac.edu/~jwotton2/PSY225/rosenthal66.pdf
A lab worker fails to note a procedural error that happened only in the control group, because it doesn't threaten the expected outcome. (Rosenthal & Fode, "Psychology of the Scientist," 1963) https://en.wikipedia.org/wi

A scientist uses true random assignment generated by computer software to place participants into treatment and control groups. (Rosenthal & Fode, "Psychology of the Scientist," 1963) https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Observer_bias
