column3: believing you see the world objectively, and people who disagree are uninformed/irrational/biased.
column4:
1. “If they disagree, they didn’t read the facts.” 
2. You think your political view is just common sense.
 3. Group argument: you assume you’re the only logical one. 
4. You treat your opinions as reality, not perspective.
 5. You’re shocked others interpret the same event differently.

Two negotiators each believe their own proposal is the objectively fair one, and assume the other side must be biased or misinformed for disagreeing. (Ross & Ward, 1996) https://web.colby.edu/cogblog/2017/04/17/naive-realism-our-misinterpretation-of-how-we-interpret-the-world/
A juror assumes a video of an incident shows exactly what happened, without considering that camera angle or editing shaped what was captured. (Ross & Ward, 1996) https://www.researchgate.net/publication/209409700_Naive_Realism_Implications_for_Social_Conflict_and_Misunderstanding
A person in a political argument assumes anyone who disagrees with them must be uninformed, lazy, or dishonest, rather than simply seeing the issue differently. (Ross & Ward, 1996) https://web.colby.edu/cogblog/2017/04/17/naive-realism-our-misinterpretation-of-how-we-interpret-the-world/
A manager assumes their read of a tense meeting is the objective truth, and concludes a coworker who saw it differently must have a hidden agenda. (Nautilus, Are You a Naive Realist?) https://nautil.us/are-you-a-naive-realist-238495
Two divorcing spouses each believe they are recalling the marriage exactly as it happened and assume the other is distorting the truth. (Ross & Ward, 1996) https://web.colby.edu/cogblog/2017/04/17/naive-realism-our-misinterpretation-of-how-we-interpret-the-world/
A survey found that people who answered "yes" to a hypothetical question also assumed most other people would answer the same way, treating their own view as the obvious default. (Ross, Greene, & House, 1977, cited via naive realism research) https://web.colby.edu/cogblog/2017/04/17/naive-realism-our-misinterpretation-of-how-we-interpret-the-world/
Two coworkers in a dispute each think they are being completely reasonable, and assume the other must be acting out of self-interest or irrationality. (Nautilus, Are You a Naive Realist?) https://nautil.us/are-you-a-naive-realist-238495
A protester assumes people who oppose their cause simply haven't seen the same facts, when in reality they have seen the facts and reached a different conclusion. (Ross & Ward, 1996) https://web.colby.edu/cogblog/2017/04/17/naive-realism-our-misinterpretation-of-how-we-interpret-the-world/
A juror who watches a video of a police stop feels they are witnessing the event directly and objectively, not through an edited and selective lens. (Ross & Ward, 1996) https://www.researchgate.net/publication/209409700_Naive_Realism_Implications_for_Social_Conflict_and_Misunderstanding
Two friends who disagree about a restaurant's quality each assume their own taste reflects the objectively correct judgment. (Nautilus, Are You a Naive Realist?) https://nautil.us/are-you-a-naive-realist-238495
A manager assumes an employee who pushes back on a plan must be under some biasing influence, since the manager is certain their own plan is simply correct. (Ross & Ward, 1996) https://web.colby.edu/cogblog/2017/04/17/naive-realism-our-misinterpretation-of-how-we-interpret-the-world/
In an international conflict, each side believes their own narrative reflects objective reality and views the other side's narrative as pure propaganda. (Nasie et al., 2014, cited via naive realism research) https://nautil.us/are-you-a-naive-realist-238495
A jury member assumes courtroom footage speaks for itself and doesn't consider how the footage was selected or framed by attorneys. (Ross & Ward, 1996) https://www.researchgate.net/publication/209409700_Naive_Realism_Implications_for_Social_Conflict_and_Misunderstanding
A parent assumes their view of a family argument is simply "what happened" and is baffled that their teenager remembers it so differently. (Ross & Ward, 1996) https://web.colby.edu/cogblog/2017/04/17/naive-realism-our-misinterpretation-of-how-we-interpret-the-world/
Two coauthors disagree about who contributed more to a paper, each convinced their own memory of the work is the accurate one. (Ross & Ward, 1996) https://web.colby.edu/cogblog/2017/04/17/naive-realism-our-misinterpretation-of-how-we-interpret-the-world/
A voter assumes that anyone who supports a different candidate simply hasn't looked at the facts as clearly as they have. (Ross & Ward, 1996) https://web.colby.edu/cogblog/2017/04/17/naive-realism-our-misinterpretation-of-how-we-interpret-the-world/
A team member assumes that their interpretation of a client's email is the obvious one, and is surprised when a colleague reads it completely differently. (Nautilus, Are You a Naive Realist?) https://nautil.us/are-you-a-naive-realist-238495
Two witnesses to the same car accident each insist their account is the accurate one, assuming the other must be misremembering. (Ross & Ward, 1996) https://web.colby.edu/cogblog/2017/04/17/naive-realism-our-misinterpretation-of-how-we-interpret-the-world/
A debate audience member assumes their side clearly won and is confused why anyone would think otherwise, treating their judgment as simply objective. (Ross & Ward, 1996) https://web.colby.edu/cogblog/2017/04/17/naive-realism-our-misinterpretation-of-how-we-interpret-the-world/
A manager reviewing a recorded meeting trusts the recording as a complete and neutral account, without questioning what the camera missed. (Ross & Ward, 1996) https://www.researchgate.net/publication/209409700_Naive_Realism_Implications_for_Social_Conflict_and_Misunderstanding
column5:
You say “This is how I see it,” instead of “This is how it is,” and you ask how others interpret it.
Two people watch the same event and disagree; you treat both views as plausible, not “one must be lying.”
You separate facts from interpretations (“He didn’t reply” vs “He doesn’t care”).
You notice your mood changes your judgment and you wait before making a final call.
You update your belief after new evidence, even if your first impression felt “obviously true.”

Two negotiators each acknowledge that their own proposal reflects one reasonable interpretation among several, not the single objective truth. (Ross & Ward, 1996) https://web.colby.edu/cogblog/2017/04/17/naive-realism-our-misinterpretation-of-how-we-interpret-the-world/
A juror considers how the camera angle and editing might have shaped a video before drawing conclusions from it. (Ross & Ward, 1996) https://www.researchgate.net/publication/209409700_Naive_Realism_Implications_for_Social_Conflict_and_Misunderstanding
A person in a political discussion asks a friend to explain their reasoning, genuinely curious why they see the issue differently. (Ross & Ward, 1996) https://web.colby.edu/cogblog/2017/04/17/naive-realism-our-misinterpretation-of-how-we-interpret-the-world/
A manager asks a coworker directly why they read a meeting differently, rather than assuming the coworker has a hidden agenda. (Nautilus, Are You a Naive Realist?) https://nautil.us/are-you-a-naive-realist-238495
Two divorcing spouses attend mediation and each acknowledge their memory of events may be shaped by their own perspective. (Ross & Ward, 1996) https://web.colby.edu/cogblog/2017/04/17/naive-realism-our-misinterpretation-of-how-we-interpret-the-world/
A survey participant predicts that other people's answers to a hypothetical question will vary widely, rather than assuming most will match their own. (Ross, Greene, & House, 1977, cited via naive realism research) https://web.colby.edu/cogblog/2017/04/17/naive-realism-our-misinterpretation-of-how-we-interpret-the-world/
Two coworkers in a dispute each consider that the other might have information or a valid perspective they themselves are missing. (Nautilus, Are You a Naive Realist?) https://nautil.us/are-you-a-naive-realist-238495
A protester researches the specific reasons opponents give for disagreeing, discovering they have seen the same facts and drawn a different conclusion in good faith. (Ross & Ward, 1996) https://web.colby.edu/cogblog/2017/04/17/naive-realism-our-misinterpretation-of-how-we-interpret-the-world/
A juror asks to see the full unedited footage of a police stop instead of assuming the clip shown captures the whole truth. (Ross & Ward, 1996) https://www.researchgate.net/publication/209409700_Naive_Realism_Implications_for_Social_Conflict_and_Misunderstanding
Two friends who disagree about a restaurant agree that taste is subjective and neither view is objectively correct. (Nautilus, Are You a Naive Realist?) https://nautil.us/are-you-a-naive-realist-238495
A manager listens to an employee's pushback and updates the plan after realizing the employee raised a valid point. (Ross & Ward, 1996) https://web.colby.edu/cogblog/2017/04/17/naive-realism-our-misinterpretation-of-how-we-interpret-the-world/
In an international conflict, mediators help each side see that the other's narrative reflects a genuinely different lived experience, not propaganda. (Nasie et al., 2014, cited via naive realism research) https://nautil.us/are-you-a-naive-realist-238495
A jury member specifically asks the judge how the courtroom footage was selected before weighing its meaning. (Ross & Ward, 1996) https://www.researchgate.net/publication/209409700_Naive_Realism_Implications_for_Social_Conflict_and_Misunderstanding
A parent asks their teenager to describe their side of an argument and accepts that their memories genuinely differ without either being "wrong." (Ross & Ward, 1996) https://web.colby.edu/cogblog/2017/04/17/naive-realism-our-misinterpretation-of-how-we-interpret-the-world/
Two coauthors review email records together to objectively determine who contributed what, rather than relying on personal memory alone. (Ross & Ward, 1996) https://web.colby.edu/cogblog/2017/04/17/naive-realism-our-misinterpretation-of-how-we-interpret-the-world/
A voter reads a rival candidate's platform in full before concluding their opponent's supporters may have reasonable, informed reasons for their choice. (Ross & Ward, 1996) https://web.colby.edu/cogblog/2017/04/17/naive-realism-our-misinterpretation-of-how-we-interpret-the-world/
A team member checks with a colleague about how they interpreted a client's email before assuming their own reading was the only reasonable one. (Nautilus, Are You a Naive Realist?) https://nautil.us/are-you-a-naive-realist-238495
Two witnesses to a car accident compare notes calmly and realize their different vantage points explain their different accounts. (Ross & Ward, 1996) https://web.colby.edu/cogblog/2017/04/17/naive-realism-our-misinterpretation-of-how-we-interpret-the-world/
A debate audience member acknowledges that reasonable people could score the debate differently depending on which arguments they valued most. (Ross & Ward, 1996) https://web.colby.edu/cogblog/2017/04/17/naive-realism-our-misinterpretation-of-how-we-interpret-the-world/
A manager reviewing a recorded meeting notes that the camera only captured part of the room and asks attendees what it might have missed. (Ross & Ward, 1996) https://www.researchgate.net/publication/209409700_Naive_Realism_Implications_for_Social_Conflict_and_Misunderstanding
